- [definition] Migrating to @openrouter/agent — Move agent toolkit imports from @openrouter/sdk to the standalone @openrouter/agent package — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/agent-migration#migrating-to-openrouteragent
- [definition] Who needs to migrate? — You need to migrate if your code imports any of the following from `@openrouter/sdk`: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/agent-migration#who-needs-to-migrate
- [definition] Step 2: Update imports — Replace `@openrouter/sdk` subpath imports with the equivalent `@openrouter/agent` subpath. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/agent-migration#step-2-update-imports
- [definition] Client class — `@openrouter/agent` ships its own `OpenRouter` client, so you can drop the `@openrouter/sdk` dependency entirely if you only use agent features: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/agent-migration#client-class
- [definition] Conversation state and message formats — Conversation helpers and message format converters are available from the package barrel: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/agent-migration#conversation-state-and-message-formats
- [definition] Step 3: Verify your build — Run your type checker and tests to confirm everything resolves correctly: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/agent-migration#step-3-verify-your-build
- [definition] Automated migration — The script below handles **subpath imports** automatically. Barrel imports (`from '@openrouter/sdk'`) and client class imports (`import OpenRouter from '@openrouter/sdk'`) must be updated **manually**. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/agent-migration#automated-migration
- [definition] Do I still need `@openrouter/sdk`? — Only if you use non-agent REST API features like `client.models.list()`, `client.credits.get()`, or `client.chat.send()`. If your code only uses `callModel`, tools, and the agent client, you can remove `@openrouter/sdk` entirely. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/agent-migration#do-i-still-need-openroutersdk
- [definition] Can I use both packages together? — Yes. They are designed to work side by side. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/agent-migration#can-i-use-both-packages-together
- [definition] Will the old imports keep working? — The agent exports will be removed from `@openrouter/sdk` in a future major version. Update your imports now to avoid a breaking change later. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/agent-migration#will-the-old-imports-keep-working
- [definition] Do I need to change my API key or configuration? — No. `@openrouter/agent` uses the same API key and endpoints. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/agent-migration#do-i-need-to-change-my-api-key-or-configuration

- [definition] Agent SDK API Reference — Type signatures and exports for the Agent SDK, covering callModel, ModelResult, tool types, conversation state helpers, stop conditions, and format utilities. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/api-reference#agent-sdk-api-reference
- [definition] ProviderPreferences — Configuration for routing and provider selection. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/api-reference#providerpreferences
- [definition] ModelResult — Wrapper providing multiple consumption patterns for a response. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/api-reference#modelresult
- [definition] HITLTool — Human-in-the-loop tool with `onToolCalled` and optional `onResponseReceived` hooks. `outputSchema` is required — it validates both the hook's non-null return value and the caller-supplied response delivered via `function_call_output`. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/api-reference#hitltool
- [definition] ToolExecuteContext — Flat context passed to tool execute functions. Merges `TurnContext` fields with tool-specific context: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/api-reference#toolexecutecontext
- [definition] ToolContextMap — Context map for `callModel`'s `context` option, keyed by tool name: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/api-reference#toolcontextmap
- [definition] ContextInput — Context can be static, a sync function, or an async function: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/api-reference#contextinput
- [definition] Conversation State — See [Tool Approval & State](/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tool-approval-state) for a walkthrough of the state accessor pattern, resumption, and status values. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/api-reference#conversation-state
- [definition] Serialization helpers — Opt-in wrappers over `JSON.stringify` / `JSON.parse` that manage the state version and surface typed errors on load. Available at the package root and via the `@openrouter/agent/conversation-state` subpath. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/api-reference#serialization-helpers
- [concept] The Agent SDK API Reference covers type signatures and exports for callModel, ModelResult, tool types, conversation state helpers, stop conditions, and format utilities. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/api-reference
- [fact] Either the `model` or `models` field is required in CallModelInput. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/api-reference
- [concept] ProviderPreferences is used for configuration regarding routing and provider selection. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/api-reference
- [fact] The `getText()` method retrieves text content after tool execution completes. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/api-reference
- [concept] The `getResponse()` method returns the full response including usage data such as inputTokens, outputTokens, and cachedTokens. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/api-reference
- [fact] The `getReasoningStream()` method streams reasoning deltas specifically for reasoning models. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/api-reference
- [concept] The `getContextUpdates()` method streams context snapshots whenever a tool calls `setContext()`, completing when tool execution finishes. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/api-reference
- [actionable] Call the `cancel()` method to cancel the stream and all consumers. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/api-reference
- [fact] The `tool()` function creates a typed tool with Zod schema validation. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/api-reference
- [problem] Omitting both `execute` and `onToolCalled` in ToolConfig (with `execute: false`) creates a manual tool. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/api-reference
- [fact] HITLTool requires an `outputSchema` to validate both the hook's non-null return value and the caller-supplied response delivered via `function_call_output`. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/api-reference
- [fact] Returning `null` from `onToolCalled` pauses the loop and sets the conversation status to `'awaiting_hitl'`. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/api-reference
- [problem] Throwing from `onToolCalled` is surfaced as a tool error of the form `{ error: ... }`. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/api-reference
- [fact] The `isManualTool` type guard returns true for tools with no `execute` and no `onToolCalled`, which always pause the loop. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/api-reference
- [fact] The `source` field was added in `@openrouter/agent` version 0.8.0, representing an additive breaking change for consumers exhaustively matching `ToolExecutionResult` payloads. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/api-reference
- [fact] The status `'awaiting_client_tools'` was added in `@openrouter/agent` version 0.8.0 for unresolved manual tool calls where `execute: false`. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/api-reference
- [concept] Serialization helpers provide opt-in wrappers over `JSON.stringify` and `JSON.parse` that manage state version and surface typed errors on load. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/api-reference
- [fact] Additive changes to serialized JSON stay within a major version, while migrations run inside `deserializeConversationState` on version bumps. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/api-reference
- [concept] The `fromChatMessages` helper converts OpenAI chat format to OpenResponses input. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/api-reference
- [concept] The `fromClaudeMessages` helper converts Anthropic Claude format to OpenResponses input. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/api-reference
- [fact] Type utilities include `InferToolInput`, `InferToolOutput`, and `InferToolEvent` for type inference. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/api-reference
- [fact] The `TypedToolCall` utility is available as part of the Type Utilities exports. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/api-reference

## Doom-Loop Detection
<https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/doom-loop-detection>

- [snippet] Overview: const result = openrouter.callModel({ — `const result = openrouter.callModel({` — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/doom-loop-detection#overview
- [snippet] Getting unstuck with a stronger model: openrouter.callModel({ — `openrouter.callModel({` — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/doom-loop-detection#getting-unstuck-with-a-stronger-model
- [snippet] Telling the detector what counts as "the same": `loopKey`: tool({ — `// Compute the identity. A web-search tool normalizes its query,` — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/doom-loop-detection#telling-the-detector-what-counts-as-the-same-loopkey
- [parameter] `observe`: Take notes only: emit the `DoomLoopDetected` hook so you can see it happened — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/doom-loop-detection#what-happens-as-the-streak-grows
- [parameter] `steer`: Nudge the agent with a message before its next turn, telling it it's repeating itself (off by default) — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/doom-loop-detection#what-happens-as-the-streak-grows
- [parameter] `escalate`: Call in help: run the next turn on a stronger model and/or a forced `openrouter:advisor` consult, then switch back (off by default; needs an `escalation` config) — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/doom-loop-detection#what-happens-as-the-streak-grows
- [parameter] `block`: Refuse to run the repeated call. The model gets an error explaining why, so it can change course. Text and server-tool repeats can't be blocked (they already happened); those fall through to the strongest weaker action you've enabled (`escalate`, `steer`, or `observe`) — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/doom-loop-detection#what-happens-as-the-streak-grows
- [parameter] `stop`: End the run before it wastes more money (`SessionEnd.reason: 'doom_loop'`). Any unfinished tool calls get clean error outputs, so the saved conversation stays valid and can be resumed — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/doom-loop-detection#what-happens-as-the-streak-grows
- [definition] Doom-Loop Detection — Detect and act on agent runs that repeat the same tool calls, server-tool requests, or text without making progress. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/doom-loop-detection#doom-loop-detection
- [definition] Overview — Sometimes an agent gets stuck. It tries the same tool call, gets the same result, and tries again anyway, like a robot vacuum bumping into the same wall forever. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/doom-loop-detection#overview
- [definition] How repeats are counted — Each time the model repeats itself, its streak grows by one. The rules for counting are simple and predictable: the same transcript always produces the same result. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/doom-loop-detection#how-repeats-are-counted
- [definition] What happens as the streak grows — You set a threshold for each action you want. When the streak reaches a threshold, that action fires, and the strongest one wins: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/doom-loop-detection#what-happens-as-the-streak-grows
- [definition] Getting unstuck with a stronger model — Instead of just blocking a stuck agent, you can give it help. With `escalate`, the next turn runs on a smarter model, then switches back to the cheap one: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/doom-loop-detection#getting-unstuck-with-a-stronger-model
- [definition] Telling the detector what counts as "the same": `loopKey` — By default, two calls count as the same when all their inputs match exactly. That default is sometimes wrong, so you can give each tool its own idea of "the same" with `loopKey`: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/doom-loop-detection#telling-the-detector-what-counts-as-the-same-loopkey
- [definition] Pausing and resuming — You don't need to worry about a model dodging detection with rearranged JSON keys or formatting changes, and a model stuck sending the same invalid JSON gets caught instead of bouncing off the parse error forever. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/doom-loop-detection#pausing-and-resuming

- [parameter] `url`: Remote MCP server endpoint. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/mcp-tools#options

- [parameter] `autoRefreshOnListChanged`: Re-list on `tools/list_changed` (default on). — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/mcp-tools#options
- [parameter] `onElicitation`: Handle server elicitation requests. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/mcp-tools#options

- [definition] MCP Tools — Connect remote Model Context Protocol servers to the Agent SDK with @openrouter/mcp (auth, caching, streaming, resources, and elicitation). — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/mcp-tools#mcp-tools
- [definition] When to use it — Reach for `@openrouter/mcp` when you want to plug an existing MCP server (Linear, GitHub, an internal tool server) into an Agent SDK loop without hand-rolling the protocol. It complements your own [`tool()`](/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tools) definitions. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/mcp-tools#when-to-use-it
- [definition] Quick start — Call `createMCPTools()` once, spread `mcp.tools` into `callModel`, and close the handle when you're done: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/mcp-tools#quick-start
- [definition] Authentication — Auth is supplied once and reused for tool discovery and every tool call. Choose the shape that matches how your MCP server expects to be called: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/mcp-tools#authentication
- [definition] Combining with your own tools — MCP tools coexist with your own `tool()` definitions. Every tool the wrapper produces is marked with the `_mcp` brand, so the Agent SDK can tell the two apart and preserve type safety on your typed results: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/mcp-tools#combining-with-your-own-tools
- [definition] The `source` discriminant — `ToolExecutionResult` (and the streaming `tool.result` event) carry `source: 'client' | 'mcp'`: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/mcp-tools#the-source-discriminant
- [definition] `isMcpTool()` and `markMcp()` — Two helpers let you interact with the brand directly: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/mcp-tools#ismcptool-and-markmcp
- [definition] Caching and rehydration — Every call to `createMCPTools()` performs an `initialize` + `tools/list` round-trip. For cold-start-heavy workloads (serverless, edge, per-request handlers) you can persist a snapshot and rebuild the handle without touching the network. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/mcp-tools#caching-and-rehydration
- [definition] Using an `MCPCacheStore` — Pass a store and key to `createMCPTools()` and it will rehydrate on hit and connect + write on miss automatically: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/mcp-tools#using-an-mcpcachestore
- [definition] Streaming, progress, and cancellation — Wrapped MCP tools behave like [generator tools](/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tools#generator-tools). Progress notifications the server emits during a tool call surface as `tool.progress` events on the same streams your own tools use: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/mcp-tools#streaming-progress-and-cancellation
- [definition] Multiple servers — Spread the tools from more than one handle to compose several MCP servers into a single agent. Use `toolNamePrefix` to keep names unambiguous: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/mcp-tools#multiple-servers
- [concept] @openrouter/mcp connects to remote Model Context Protocol servers via Streamable HTTP or SSE and exposes their tools as first-class callModel tools. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/mcp-tools
- [problem] The @openrouter/mcp package intentionally excludes support for stdio MCP servers, targeting only remote servers reachable over HTTP. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/mcp-tools
- [fact] MCP tools and locally-defined tool() definitions can coexist in the same tools array, distinguished by a source discriminant. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/mcp-tools
- [actionable] Call createMCPTools() once to get a handle containing mcp.tools, mcp.serialize(), and mcp.close(). — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/mcp-tools
- [concept] The mcp.serialize() method captures the current tool list and optionally credentials as JSON for cache reuse. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/mcp-tools
- [idea] Prefer an OAuthClientProvider over caching a static bearer token when the server supports OAuth to allow automatic token refresh. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/mcp-tools
- [fact] Wrapped MCP tools are marked with an _mcp brand, allowing the Agent SDK to distinguish them from client-defined tools. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/mcp-tools
- [problem] MCP tool results are typed as unknown because the MCP server describes output at runtime, which can collapse result unions without narrowing. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/mcp-tools
- [actionable] Use isMcpTool(tool) as a runtime type guard to treat MCP tools differently in lifecycle hooks or custom stop conditions. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/mcp-tools
- [actionable] Use markMcp(tool) to add the _mcp brand to an already-built client tool, though this is rarely needed manually. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/mcp-tools
- [fact] Every call to createMCPTools() performs an initialize + tools/list round-trip by default. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/mcp-tools
- [idea] For serverless or edge workloads, persist a serialized snapshot to rebuild the handle without network calls during cold starts. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/mcp-tools
- [problem] When cacheCredentials is enabled, snapshots contain bearer tokens or headers and must be stored securely as a secret store. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/mcp-tools
- [actionable] Implement an MCPCacheStore with get, set, and delete methods to back the cache with Redis, a database, or any KV store. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/mcp-tools
- [concept] Wrapped MCP tools behave like generator tools, surfacing progress notifications as tool.progress events on the same streams. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/mcp-tools

- [definition] getNewMessagesStream() — `getNewMessagesStream()` is deprecated. Use `getItemsStream()` instead, which includes all item types and follows the items-based paradigm. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/streaming#getnewmessagesstream

- [fact] Each iteration of getItemsStream() yields a complete item with the same ID but updated content. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/streaming

- [concept] getToolStream() streams tool deltas and preliminary results. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/streaming
- [fact] Multiple consumers can read from the same result using the underlying ReusableReadableStream. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/streaming
- [actionable] Cancel a stream to stop generation by calling the cancel method on the stream. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/streaming
- [idea] Use getItemsStream() instead of getNewMessagesStream() because it includes all item types and follows the items-based paradigm. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/streaming

- [parameter] `'awaiting_client_tools'`: Paused because one or more [manual tools](/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tools#manual-tools) (`execute: false` / no execute fn) were called but not resolved. The unresolved calls are stored in `pendingToolCalls`. Resume by calling `callModel` again with new `input`; this clears the stale pendings and continues as a normal turn. Unlike `awaiting_approval` and… — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tool-approval-state#status-values
- [parameter] `'awaiting_async_tools'`: Paused by a [deferred tool](/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/async-tools) whose `run` called `ctx.defer(taskId)`. Any process can settle the task via `.resolve()` / `.fail()` / `.cancel()` (or `resumeToolResults`). To continue the conversation immediately, pass `run` when settling; omitting `run` only records the result and delivers it on the next `callModel({ state })` call.… — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tool-approval-state#status-values
- [parameter] `'complete'`: Conversation finished normally — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tool-approval-state#status-values
- [parameter] `'interrupted'`: Conversation was interrupted and can be resumed — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tool-approval-state#status-values
- [definition] Tool Approval & State Persistence — Add human-in-the-loop approval gates for sensitive tools and persist conversation state across callModel invocations. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tool-approval-state#tool-approval-state-persistence
- [definition] Why Approval Gates? — Some tools — sending emails, making payments, deleting records — should not auto-execute without human review. The SDK provides two mechanisms to control this: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tool-approval-state#why-approval-gates
- [definition] Tool-Level Approval — Add `requireApproval` directly on a tool definition. It accepts a boolean or a function: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tool-approval-state#tool-level-approval
- [definition] Conditional Approval — Pass a function to require approval only in certain cases: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tool-approval-state#conditional-approval

- [definition] How the Approval Flow Works — When tools with approval gates are called by the model, the SDK follows this flow: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tool-approval-state#how-the-approval-flow-works
- [definition] StateAccessor Interface — The `StateAccessor` interface enables any storage backend: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tool-approval-state#stateaccessor-interface
- [definition] ConversationState — The state object tracks everything needed to resume a conversation: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tool-approval-state#conversationstate
- [definition] Serialization & Versioning — `ConversationState` carries an optional `version` field that identifies the serialization contract of the blob. `createInitialState` stamps `version: 1`; older states without the field are treated as version `1`. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tool-approval-state#serialization-versioning
- [definition] Complete Example — Here is an end-to-end example showing approval gates with state persistence: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tool-approval-state#complete-example
- [definition] Resuming from Approval — When the state has `status: 'awaiting_approval'`, pass `approveToolCalls` and/or `rejectToolCalls` to resume: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tool-approval-state#resuming-from-approval
- [definition] Resuming from Interruption — If a conversation was interrupted (`status: 'interrupted'`), calling `callModel` with the same state resumes automatically. The SDK clears the interruption flag and continues where it left off: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tool-approval-state#resuming-from-interruption
- [definition] Multi-Run Conversations — Messages accumulate automatically across `callModel` runs that share the same `StateAccessor`. Each run appends its input and response to the state's message history: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tool-approval-state#multi-run-conversations
- [concept] The SDK provides two mechanisms for human-in-the-loop workflows: `requireApproval` to pause execution of sensitive tools and `StateAccessor` to persist conversation state across invocations. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tool-approval-state
- [concept] `requireApproval` accepts a boolean or a function that receives parsed tool arguments and a `TurnContext`, returning a boolean or `Promise<boolean>`. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tool-approval-state
- [fact] A call-level `requireApproval` callback on `callModel` takes priority over tool-level `requireApproval` settings when both are present. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tool-approval-state
- [concept] When tools with approval gates are called, the SDK partitions them into two groups: those requiring approval and those that can auto-execute in parallel. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tool-approval-state
- [fact] The conversation state updates to `status: 'awaiting_approval'` when pending tool calls are stored for human review. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tool-approval-state
- [actionable] Check `result.requiresApproval()` and inspect pending calls using `result.getPendingToolCalls()` after a model call to determine if human intervention is needed. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tool-approval-state
- [actionable] Resume a paused conversation by calling `callModel` again with the same `state`, passing `approveToolCalls` and/or `rejectToolCalls` arrays of tool call IDs. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tool-approval-state
- [fact] Rejected tools send an error message to the model explaining the rejection, while approved tools execute and send results back to the model. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tool-approval-state
- [concept] The `StateAccessor` interface enables any storage backend, with in-memory implementation provided for development and persistent backends like Redis or databases recommended for production. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tool-approval-state
- [fact] `ConversationState` carries an optional `version` field that identifies the serialization contract, with `createInitialState` stamping `version: 1`. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tool-approval-state
- [fact] Older states without a version field are treated as version `1` for backward compatibility. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tool-approval-state
- [idea] Use the opt-in helpers for serialization to get typed errors and a migration hook for future changes rather than relying solely on `JSON.stringify` / `JSON.parse`. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tool-approval-state
- [fact] The compatibility policy treats serialized JSON as opaque, allowing additive field changes within a major version but prohibiting introspection of item shapes across releases. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tool-approval-state
- [fact] On version bumps, migration work runs inside `deserializeConversationState`, allowing consumers using helpers to get forward-compatibility automatically. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tool-approval-state
- [problem] `UnsupportedStateVersionError` is thrown if the blob's version is not in the SDK build's supported set, exposing `{ found, supported }` for logging. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tool-approval-state
- [problem] `InvalidStateError` occurs if the payload is malformed JSON or missing required fields: `id`, `messages`, `status`, `createdAt`, or `updatedAt`. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tool-approval-state
- [fact] When resuming from an interruption (`status: 'interrupted'`), calling `callModel` with the same state automatically clears the flag and continues where it left off. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tool-approval-state
- [fact] Messages accumulate automatically across `callModel` runs that share the same `StateAccessor`, with each run appending input and response to the message history. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tool-approval-state

- [concept] The SDK supports four types of tools: regular, generator, manual, and Human-in-the-Loop (HITL), with automatic multi-turn execution. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tools
- [fact] Generator tools require an eventSchema to enable progress updates, which are streamed via getToolStream() and getFullResponsesStream(). — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tools
- [problem] If manual tool calls remain unresolved at the end of a round, the loop pauses and persists them to ConversationState.pendingToolCalls with status 'awaiting_client_tools'. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tools
- [actionable] To resume a paused manual tool round, call callModel again with new input to clear stale pendings and proceed as a normal turn. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tools
- [concept] HITL tools extend manual semantics with onToolCalled and onResponseReceived hooks to decide per call whether to respond programmatically or pause for human input. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tools
- [fact] An outputSchema is required for HITL tools to validate both the onToolCalled return value and values delivered via function_call_output. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tools
- [problem] When onToolCalled returns null, the conversation state moves to status 'awaiting_hitl' and requires a function_call_output item in the input to resume. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tools
- [idea] Use HITL tools for data-driven decisions like amount thresholds or risk scoring, whereas requireApproval is better for explicit human consent. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tools
- [fact] The source field in tool.result events was added in @openrouter/agent version 0.8.0 as an additive breaking change. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tools
- [actionable] Narrow on source === 'client' to recover schema-derived result types when mixing MCP tools with fully-typed local tools. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tools
- [fact] The markMcp helper brands a tool as originating from an MCP server, while @openrouter/mcp automatically brands its wrapped tools. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tools
- [concept] Context can be declared via contextSchema to receive typed, persistent data keyed by tool name that persists across turns. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tools
- [actionable] Use resolveContext for one-time initialization at turn 0, and setContext() inside execute functions for per-turn mutations. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tools
- [concept] The context.local getter is scoped to one tool, while context.shared is visible to all tools and persists across turns. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tools
- [actionable] Use getContextUpdates() on ModelResult to observe context mutations in real time. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tools
- [fact] Setting maxToolRounds: 0 disables automatic execution, returning raw tool calls instead. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tools
- [actionable] Use a function for maxToolRounds to dynamically control execution rounds based on TurnContext logic. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tools
- [fact] When the model calls multiple tools, they execute in parallel automatically. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tools
- [concept] Tool execution errors are caught and sent back to the model, while validation errors for invalid arguments are caught before execution. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tools
- [idea] Design tools to be idempotent so they can be safely re-executed without side effects. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tools
- [actionable] Wrap long-running operations with timeout handling to prevent hanging executions. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/agent-sdk/call-model/tools

- [definition] What are embeddings? — Embeddings transform text into high-dimensional vectors where semantically similar texts are positioned closer together in vector space. For example, "cat" and "kitten" would have similar embeddings, while "cat" and "airplane" would be far apart. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/embeddings#what-are-embeddings
- [definition] Common use cases — Embeddings are used in a wide variety of applications: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/embeddings#common-use-cases
- [definition] Basic request — To generate embeddings, send a POST request to `/embeddings` with your text input and chosen model: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/embeddings#basic-request
- [definition] Batch processing — You can generate embeddings for multiple texts in a single request by passing an array of strings: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/embeddings#batch-processing
- [definition] Image input — Some embedding models support image inputs, enabling multimodal embeddings that capture visual content alongside text. This is useful for image search, visual similarity, and cross-modal retrieval tasks. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/embeddings#image-input
- [definition] API reference — For detailed information about request parameters, response format, and all available options, see the [Embeddings API Reference](/docs/api/api-reference/embeddings/submit-an-embedding-request). — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/embeddings#api-reference
- [definition] Available models — OpenRouter provides access to various embedding models from different providers. You can view all available embedding models at: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/embeddings#available-models

- [definition] Provider routing — You can control which providers serve your embedding requests using the `provider` parameter. This is useful for: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/embeddings#provider-routing

- [parameter] `payment_required`: HTTP Status=The account or API key has insufficient credits. [Add credits](https://openrouter.ai/credits) and retry. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#authentication-and-authorization

- [definition] Retry-After header — On  and  responses, OpenRouter may include a standard HTTP `Retry-After` response header indicating how many seconds to wait before retrying. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#retry-after-header

- [definition] Guardrail errors — On inference endpoints (`/chat/completions`, `/responses`, `/messages`), a request can be blocked before it reaches a provider — for example by a content filter or prompt-injection detector configured via [guardrails](/docs/guides/features/guardrails). — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#guardrail-errors
- [definition] Provider errors — OpenRouter normalizes every upstream provider error into the stable, typed `error_type` vocabulary documented under [Typed Error Codes](#typed-error-codes). — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#provider-errors
- [definition] Masking and raw provider details — When a request fails with a `500`, the `message` is replaced with a generic string and `provider_code` and `openrouter_metadata` are omitted, but `error_type` is still present (`server`). — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#masking-and-raw-provider-details
- [definition] When no content is generated — Occasionally, the model may not generate any content. This typically occurs when: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#when-no-content-is-generated
- [definition] Streaming error formats — When using streaming mode (`stream: true`), errors are handled differently depending on when they occur: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#streaming-error-formats
- [definition] Pre-stream errors — Errors that occur before any tokens are sent follow the standard error format above, with appropriate HTTP status codes. At this stage the HTTP response hasn't been committed yet, so OpenRouter can: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#pre-stream-errors
- [definition] Mid-stream errors — Once the first token has been written to the client, the HTTP `200 OK` status and headers are already committed — they can't be changed. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#mid-stream-errors
- [definition] Typed error codes — When a provider error reaches your application, OpenRouter tags it with a canonical `error_type` string — both on the non-streaming response body and on mid-stream SSE events. Use this value, not the HTTP status code alone, to programmatically distinguish error categories. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#typed-error-codes
- [definition] Skin-specific error formats — OpenRouter exposes three API skins. Each translates the same internal provider error types into its own wire format, for non-streaming responses and in-stream errors alike. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#skin-specific-error-formats
- [definition] Chat Completions (`/api/v1/chat/completions`) — Mid-stream errors appear as a `chat.completion.chunk` with a top-level `error` object (shape shown [above](#mid-stream-errors)). The `error.metadata.error_type` field carries the typed code. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#chat-completions-apiv1chatcompletions
- [definition] Responses API (`/api/v1/responses`) — The Responses API maps internal error types to the OpenAI Responses error code set. The mapping is narrower — many distinct internal types collapse to `server_error` — so the precise reason is preserved in a top-level `error_type` field on the response, outside the native `error` object: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#responses-api-apiv1responses
- [definition] Anthropic Messages (`/api/v1/messages`) — The Anthropic Messages skin maps internal types to Anthropic-native error type strings: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#anthropic-messages-apiv1messages
- [definition] Debugging — OpenRouter provides a `debug` option that allows you to inspect the exact request body that was sent to the upstream provider. This works with both the Chat Completions API (`/api/v1/chat/completions`) and the Responses API (`/api/v1/responses`). — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#debugging
- [definition] Debug option shape — The debug option is an object with the following shape: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#debug-option-shape
- [definition] Usage — To enable debug output, include the `debug` parameter in your request: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#usage
- [definition] Use cases — The debug output is particularly useful for: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#use-cases
- [definition] Privacy and redaction — OpenRouter will make a best effort to automatically redact potentially sensitive or noisy data from debug output. Remember that the debug option is not intended for production. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#privacy-and-redaction
- [concept] The Retry-After header indicates how many seconds to wait before retrying on specific responses. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#retry-after-header
- [fact] OpenRouter includes the standard HTTP Retry-After response header on 429 and 503 responses. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#retry-after-header
- [concept] The OpenAI SDK, Anthropic SDK, Vercel AI SDK, and OpenRouter SDK automatically respect the Retry-After header for backoff. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#retry-after-header
- [actionable] If using fetch directly, honor the Retry-After header before retrying by reading the response headers. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#retry-after-header
- [concept] Guardrail errors occur when a request is blocked on inference endpoints before reaching a provider, such as by a content filter or prompt-injection detector. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#guardrail-errors
- [fact] On `/chat/completions` and `/responses` endpoints, a guardrail block returns an HTTP `403` status code with a message describing the block reason. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#guardrail-errors
- [fact] On the `/messages` endpoint, a guardrail block is returned as an Anthropic `permission_error` envelope rather than a standard OpenRouter body. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#guardrail-errors
- [fact] When the `X-OpenRouter-Experimental-Metadata: enabled` header is used, the `403` response includes a full `openrouter_metadata` object. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#guardrail-errors
- [fact] The `openrouter_metadata` object in a guardrail error response contains routing context and a `pipeline` array detailing the specific guardrail stages that ran. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#guardrail-errors
- [concept] The structure of the `openrouter_metadata` object in error responses follows the same shape as it does on successful responses. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#guardrail-errors
- [concept] OpenRouter normalizes every upstream provider error into the stable, typed `error_type` vocabulary. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#provider-errors
- [fact] The same `error_type` values describe what went wrong whether the provider error arrives in a non-streaming response body or as a mid-stream SSE event. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#provider-errors
- [concept] Native protocol codes like Anthropic `error.type` and Responses `error.code` are best-effort and can differ between formats. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#provider-errors
- [idea] Developers should rely on the `error_type` field across all provider formats rather than native protocol codes. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#provider-errors
- [fact] For Chat Completions, a provider error that interrupts generation carries `error_type` inside `error.metadata`. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#provider-errors
- [problem] When a request fails with a 500 status, the `message` is replaced with a generic string. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#provider-errors
- [fact] On 500 errors, `provider_code` and `openrouter_metadata` are omitted from the response. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#provider-errors
- [fact] Even when masked by a 500 error, the `error_type` field is still present with the value `server`. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#provider-errors
- [fact] For non-500 errors, the upstream provider's own error code is surfaced in `error.metadata.provider_code` when available. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#provider-errors
- [actionable] Set the `X-OpenRouter-Metadata` header to include opt-in routing context in the `openrouter_metadata` object. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#provider-errors
- [fact] The `openrouter_metadata` object contains routing summary fields such as which provider was selected and fallback attempts. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#provider-errors
- [concept] Pre-stream errors occur before any tokens are sent, allowing OpenRouter to return proper HTTP error status codes or silently retry with a different provider endpoint. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#streaming-error-formats
- [fact] Mid-stream errors occur after the first token is written, at which point the HTTP 200 OK status and headers are committed and cannot be changed. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#streaming-error-formats
- [problem] If a provider fails after partial content is delivered, OpenRouter cannot silently fail over to another provider because the stream has already started. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#streaming-error-formats
- [fact] Mid-stream errors are sent in-band as Server-Sent Events (SSE) containing both error details and a completion choice. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#streaming-error-formats
- [concept] The SSE structure for mid-stream errors includes the error at the top level alongside standard response fields. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#streaming-error-formats
- [fact] The `error.metadata.error_type` field carries a typed code that can be switched on programmatically to identify specific error categories. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#streaming-error-formats
- [fact] A `choices` array is included in mid-stream errors with `finish_reason: "error"` to properly terminate the stream. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#streaming-error-formats
- [problem] On 500-class errors, the `error.message` is replaced with a generic string and `provider_code` is omitted to prevent leaking upstream details. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#streaming-error-formats
- [fact] Common causes of mid-stream errors include provider disconnects, timeouts, token limits being hit, output content filters, and provider overload. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#streaming-error-formats
- [fact] Pre-stream errors are typically seen for issues like invalid API keys, malformed requests, or when every available provider endpoint is exhausted. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#streaming-error-formats
- [idea] Developers should check `error.metadata.error_type` to programmatically handle specific mid-stream error scenarios. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#streaming-error-formats
- [concept] OpenRouter tags provider errors with a canonical error_type string on both non-streaming response bodies and mid-stream SSE events. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#typed-error-codes
- [fact] The error_type value is stable across all three API skins even when the native protocol code is lossy. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#typed-error-codes
- [concept] Developers should use the error_type value, not the HTTP status code alone, to programmatically distinguish error categories. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#typed-error-codes
- [fact] For Chat Completions, the error_type appears at error.metadata.error_type on mid-stream error chunks and non-streaming responses. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#typed-error-codes
- [fact] For Anthropic Messages, the error_type is located at error.error_type on the SSE error event and the non-streaming error envelope. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#typed-error-codes
- [fact] For Responses, the error_type appears as a top-level field on failed responses for both streaming response.failed events and non-streaming JSON bodies. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#typed-error-codes
- [fact] The HTTP status each error_type maps to is listed in specific tables within the documentation. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#typed-error-codes
- [concept] The `debug` option allows users to inspect the exact request body sent to upstream providers, working with both Chat Completions and Responses APIs. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#debugging
- [fact] The debug option only functions when streaming mode is enabled (`stream: true`); non-streaming requests will ignore the parameter. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#debugging
- [problem] The debug flag should not be used in production environments because it may return sensitive information intended to remain hidden. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#debugging
- [fact] When `debug.echo_upstream_body` is true, a debug chunk appears as the first chunk in the streaming response with an empty `choices` array. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#debugging
- [fact] On the Responses API, debug data is delivered as a `response.debug` Server-Sent Events (SSE) event. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#debugging
- [actionable] To enable debug output, include the `debug` parameter in your request body for either Chat Completions or Responses APIs. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#debugging
- [idea] Use the debug output to understand how OpenRouter maps parameters like `max_tokens` and `temperature` to provider-specific formats. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#debugging
- [idea] Verify message formatting by checking how OpenRouter combines system messages or merges user messages for different providers. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#debugging
- [idea] Check applied defaults by observing the debug output when specific parameters are omitted from your request. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#debugging
- [idea] Debug provider fallbacks by reviewing the debug chunk sent for each attempted provider to see which were tried and what parameters were used. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#debugging
- [fact] OpenRouter attempts to automatically redact potentially sensitive or noisy data from the debug output. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#debugging
- [concept] The debug option is an object designed to inspect request transformations for different providers via the Chat Completions and Responses APIs. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging#debugging

- [definition] CompletionsResponse format — OpenRouter normalizes the schema across models and providers to comply with the [OpenAI Chat API](https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/chat). — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/overview#completionsresponse-format
- [definition] Finish reason — OpenRouter normalizes each model's `finish_reason` to one of the following values: `tool_calls`, `stop`, `length`, `content_filter`, `error`. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/overview#finish-reason
- [definition] Querying cost and stats — The token counts returned in the completions API response are calculated using the model's native tokenizer. Credit usage and model pricing are based on these native token counts. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/overview#querying-cost-and-stats
- [concept] OpenRouter normalizes request and response schemas across models and providers to match the OpenAI Chat API format. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/overview
- [fact] The complete API specification is available in YAML at https://openrouter.ai/openapi.yaml and JSON at https://openrouter.ai/openapi.json. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/overview
- [actionable] Send a POST request to the /api/v1/chat/completions endpoint with the request body defined by the TypeScript schema. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/overview
- [concept] The response_format parameter enforces structured JSON responses via two modes: basic JSON mode and strict schema mode. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/overview
- [fact] Basic JSON mode uses { type: 'json_object' } while strict schema mode uses { type: 'json_schema', json_schema: { ... } }. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/overview
- [fact] Models supporting structured outputs can be found on the models page filtered by supported_parameters=structured_outputs. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/overview
- [concept] Plugins extend model capabilities and are enabled by adding a plugins array to the request body. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/overview
- [fact] Available plugins include web, file-parser, response-healing, and context-compression. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/overview
- [actionable] Include the HTTP-Referer header to identify your app on openrouter.ai. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/overview
- [fact] The X-OpenRouter-Title header sets or modifies the app's title, and X-Title is also accepted as an alias. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/overview
- [fact] The X-OpenRouter-Categories header assigns marketplace categories to the app. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/overview
- [concept] If the model parameter is omitted, the user or payer's default model is used; otherwise, the organization prefix must be included. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/overview
- [fact] OpenRouter selects the least expensive and best GPUs available, falling back to other providers or GPUs on 5xx errors or rate limits. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/overview
- [actionable] Enable streaming for all models by setting stream: true in the request body. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/overview
- [fact] The SSE stream may contain comment payloads which should be ignored. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/overview
- [problem] Non-standard parameters like logit_bias or top_k are ignored if the chosen model does not support them, while other parameters are forwarded. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/overview
- [actionable] To guide a model's response, include a message with role: "assistant" at the end of the messages array. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/overview
- [fact] The choices property is always an array in the response, even if only one completion is returned. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/overview
- [fact] Each choice contains a delta property for streaming responses and a message property for non-streaming responses. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/overview
- [fact] Finish reasons are normalized to tool_calls, stop, length, content_filter, or error. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/overview
- [fact] Raw finish reason strings from the model are available via the native_finish_reason property. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/overview
- [concept] Token counts are calculated using the model's native tokenizer and serve as the basis for credit usage and pricing. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/overview
- [actionable] Query generation stats including cost by sending a request to the /api/v1/generation endpoint using the response id. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/overview
- [fact] Token counts are available in the usage field of the response body for non-streaming completions. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/overview

- [definition] Streaming — The OpenRouter API allows streaming responses from *any model*. This is useful for building chat interfaces or other applications where the UI should update as the model generates the response. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/streaming#streaming
- [definition] Additional information — For SSE (Server-Sent Events) streams, OpenRouter occasionally sends comments to prevent connection timeouts. These comments look like: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/streaming#additional-information
- [definition] The final usage chunk (Chat Completions) — On the Chat Completions endpoint (`/api/v1/chat/completions`), every stream ends with an extra chunk that carries the `usage` object for the request, sent just before the `[DONE]` message. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/streaming#the-final-usage-chunk-chat-completions
- [definition] Stream cancellation — Streaming requests can be cancelled by aborting the connection. For supported providers, this immediately stops model processing and billing. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/streaming#stream-cancellation
- [definition] Handling errors during streaming — OpenRouter handles errors differently depending on when they occur during the streaming process: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/streaming#handling-errors-during-streaming

## API Versioning
<https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/versioning>

- [snippet] Current version: https://openrouter.ai/api/v1 — `https://openrouter.ai/api/v1` — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/versioning#current-version
- [definition] API Versioning — How the OpenRouter API is versioned, what we consider a breaking change, and how deprecations are communicated. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/versioning#api-versioning
- [definition] Current version — The OpenRouter API has a single stable version, `v1`, selected by the URL path: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/versioning#current-version
- [definition] How the API evolves — The API changes continuously rather than in numbered releases. Every change is reflected in the [OpenAPI specification](/docs/api_reference/overview), and every release that changes the specification produces an entry in the [API Changelog](/docs/changelog). — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/versioning#how-the-api-evolves
- [definition] Nullable response fields — A response field that is present but `null` means the value is genuinely absent. Read `null` as "not set" and handle it explicitly. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/versioning#nullable-response-fields
- [definition] Deprecations — When part of the API is deprecated, the deprecation is announced in the [API Changelog](/docs/changelog) and the affected endpoint or field is marked as deprecated in the API Reference. Removal of a deprecated feature is a breaking change and follows the breaking-change process above. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/versioning#deprecations
- [concept] The OpenRouter API uses a single stable version, `v1`, selected via the URL path. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/versioning
- [fact] There are no version headers or date-based version pinning in the OpenRouter API. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/versioning
- [concept] The API evolves continuously rather than through numbered releases, with changes reflected in the OpenAPI specification and API Changelog. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/versioning
- [idea] Write clients defensively by ignoring response fields you do not recognize and failing on unknown enum values. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/versioning
- [fact] Non-breaking changes, such as new schemas or optional properties, ship without prior notice. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/versioning
- [concept] Breaking changes are reviewed by a human before publication and appear in the changelog under the **Breaking** tag with migration notes. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/versioning
- [problem] Removing or renaming an endpoint, parameter, or response field constitutes a breaking change. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/versioning
- [problem] Changing a field's type is considered a breaking change. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/versioning
- [problem] Widening a response field to allow `null` when it was previously always present is treated as a breaking change. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/versioning
- [problem] Making an optional parameter required is considered a breaking change. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/versioning
- [concept] A response field that is present but `null` means the value is genuinely absent and should be read as 'not set'. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/versioning
- [idea] Do not substitute a default value or assume `null` implies any particular fallback when handling response fields. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/versioning
- [fact] `workspace_id` is `null` on a BYOK credential that is not scoped to any workspace or on guardrails created before workspace scoping existed. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/versioning
- [problem] Assuming `null` implies a default or that a `null` guardrail applies to every workspace is incorrect. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/versioning
- [fact] Deprecations are announced in the API Changelog and the affected endpoint or field is marked as deprecated in the API Reference. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/versioning
- [fact] Removal of a deprecated feature is a breaking change that follows the standard breaking-change process. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/versioning
- [concept] Model availability is separate from API versioning, as models are added and removed by providers independently. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/versioning
- [idea] Subscribe to the RSS feed or watch the API Changelog to stay up to date with changes. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/versioning
- [idea] Filter changelog entries by the **Breaking** tag to review only compatibility-affecting changes. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/versioning

- [definition] App Attribution — Get your app featured in OpenRouter rankings and analytics — https://openrouter.ai/docs/app-attribution#app-attribution
- [definition] Benefits of app attribution — When you properly attribute your app usage, you gain access to: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/app-attribution#benefits-of-app-attribution
- [definition] Attribution headers — OpenRouter tracks app attribution through the following HTTP headers: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/app-attribution#attribution-headers
- [definition] HTTP-Referer (required) — The `HTTP-Referer` header identifies your app's URL and is used as the primary identifier for rankings. **This header is required for app attribution.** Without it, no app page will be created and your usage will not appear in rankings. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/app-attribution#http-referer-required
- [definition] X-OpenRouter-Title — The `X-OpenRouter-Title` header sets or modifies your app's display name in rankings and analytics. `X-Title` is still supported for backwards compatibility. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/app-attribution#x-openrouter-title
- [definition] X-OpenRouter-Categories — The `X-OpenRouter-Categories` header assigns your app to one or more marketplace categories. Pass a comma-separated list of up to  categories per request. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/app-attribution#x-openrouter-categories
- [definition] App rankings — Your attributed app will appear in OpenRouter's main rankings page at [openrouter.ai/rankings](https://openrouter.ai/rankings). The rankings show: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/app-attribution#app-rankings
- [definition] Model apps tabs — On individual model pages (e.g., [GPT-4o](https://openrouter.ai/models/openai/gpt-4o)), your app will be featured in the "Apps" tab showing: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/app-attribution#model-apps-tabs
- [definition] Individual app analytics — Once your app is tracked, you can access detailed analytics at `openrouter.ai/apps?url=<your-app-url>` including: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/app-attribution#individual-app-analytics
- [concept] App attribution allows developers to associate their API usage with their application, enabling visibility in OpenRouter's public rankings and detailed analytics. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/app-attribution
- [fact] The HTTP-Referer header is required for app attribution; without it, no app page will be created and usage will not appear in rankings. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/app-attribution
- [fact] The HTTP-Referer header identifies your app's URL and serves as the unique identifier for the system. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/app-attribution
- [concept] The X-OpenRouter-Title header sets or modifies your app's display name in rankings and analytics. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/app-attribution
- [fact] The X-Title header is still supported for backwards compatibility but does not create an app page on its own. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/app-attribution
- [problem] Setting only X-OpenRouter-Title without a URL will not create an app entry or appear in rankings. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/app-attribution
- [fact] The X-OpenRouter-Categories header assigns your app to one or more marketplace categories via a comma-separated list. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/app-attribution
- [fact] Categories must be lowercase, hyphen-separated, and each category is limited to 30 characters. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/app-attribution
- [problem] OpenRouter drops unrecognized categories without an error message. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/app-attribution
- [fact] Categories are merged with any existing ones, up to a total limit per request. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/app-attribution
- [idea] For localhost development, apps must include both the HTTP-Referer header and the X-OpenRouter-Title header to be tracked. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/app-attribution
- [fact] Attributed apps appear in OpenRouter's main rankings page at openrouter.ai/rankings with daily, weekly, and monthly views. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/app-attribution
- [fact] On individual model pages, apps are featured in the 'Apps' tab showing which apps use that specific model most. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/app-attribution
- [concept] Detailed analytics for a tracked app are accessible at openrouter.ai/apps?url=<your-app-url>. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/app-attribution
- [idea] Use your app's primary domain (e.g., https://myapp.com) for the HTTP-Referer header rather than subdomains unless they represent distinct apps. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/app-attribution
- [idea] Avoid generic names like 'AI App' or 'Chatbot' for the X-OpenRouter-Title; use your app's actual name instead. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/app-attribution
- [fact] Only public apps that send headers are included in rankings, and attribution headers do not expose sensitive information about requests. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/app-attribution
- [concept] The Coding category group includes tools for software development such as cli-agent, ide-extension, and cloud-agent. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/app-attribution
- [concept] The Creative category group includes apps like creative-writing, video-gen, image-gen, and audio-gen. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/app-attribution
- [concept] The Productivity category group includes writing-assistant, general-chat, personal-agent, and legal tools. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/app-attribution
- [concept] The Entertainment category group includes roleplay apps and game apps. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/app-attribution
- [idea] If a use case does not fit existing categories, developers should reach out to OpenRouter as new categories may be added in the future. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/app-attribution

- [parameter] `endpoint`: The API shape used by every request in the batch. Choose `/v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/responses`, `/v1/messages`, or `/v1/embeddings`. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/batch-quickstart#submit-a-batch
- [parameter] `model`: An OpenRouter model slug, such as `openai/gpt-4o`. This batch-level model is applied to every request. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/batch-quickstart#submit-a-batch
- [parameter] `requests`: A non-empty array of `{ custom_id, body }` items. `custom_id` must be unique within the batch, and `body` follows the shape of the selected `endpoint`. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/batch-quickstart#submit-a-batch
- [definition] Batch API Quickstart — Submit and retrieve asynchronous batches of inference requests — https://openrouter.ai/docs/batch-quickstart#batch-api-quickstart
- [definition] Limitations — The Batch API is currently text-only. On `/v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/responses`, and `/v1/messages`, validation rejects any request that carries image, audio, video, or file content parts. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/batch-quickstart#limitations
- [definition] Pricing — Batch requests are typically billed at 50% of the model's standard per-token pricing, mirroring the batch discounts offered by [OpenAI](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/batch) and [Anthropic](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/batch-processing). — https://openrouter.ai/docs/batch-quickstart#pricing
- [definition] BYOK — If you have a [provider key](/docs/guides/overview/auth/byok) configured, batches route through it automatically, the same as sync requests: the provider bills you directly for inference and OpenRouter charges only the BYOK fee (see Pricing above). Completed batches report `usage.is_byok: true`. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/batch-quickstart#byok
- [definition] Poll for results — Use the batch ID to retrieve the current status: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/batch-quickstart#poll-for-results
- [definition] Reporting issues — Each completed result's `response.body.id` is that request's OpenRouter generation ID (for example `gen-batch-...`). To flag a bad generation, copy that ID and submit it through [Report Feedback](/docs/guides/overview/report-feedback) using the **By generation ID** flow. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/batch-quickstart#reporting-issues
- [definition] Use different API shapes — Set the top-level `endpoint` to choose the request shape used by every `body` in the batch. Supported shapes: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/batch-quickstart#use-different-api-shapes
- [definition] Embeddings — Embeddings are rolling out on providers that support them. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/batch-quickstart#embeddings
- [concept] The Batch API allows submitting many inference requests together and retrieving results asynchronously within a 24-hour completion window. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/batch-quickstart
- [fact] A successful batch submission returns HTTP 202 Accepted with status 'validating', indicating the batch is persisted and queued for validation, not that all requests are complete. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/batch-quickstart
- [problem] The Batch API is text-only; it rejects any request containing image, audio, video, or file content parts on /v1/chat/completions, /v1/responses, and /v1/messages. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/batch-quickstart
- [problem] On /v1/chat/completions, requests asking for non-text output via modalities, audio, or image_config are rejected by the Batch API. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/batch-quickstart
- [fact] For embeddings on the Batch API, the input must be strings or token arrays; multimodal inputs and provider preferences are not supported. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/batch-quickstart
- [idea] Send multimodal requests to the sync API instead of using the Batch API. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/batch-quickstart
- [fact] Batch requests are typically billed at 50% of the model's standard per-token pricing, though web-search calls bill at standard rates and prompt-caching rates vary. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/batch-quickstart
- [fact] For BYOK-routed batches, usage.cost reports only the OpenRouter BYOK fee since the provider bills the user directly for inference. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/batch-quickstart
- [concept] Google Vertex uses a bucket in your GCP project for provider input and output, which OpenRouter can create automatically if the bucket field is omitted. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/batch-quickstart
- [actionable] Serialize endpoint and model before requests in the JSON body to allow stream-parsing; placing requests first returns a 400 error. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/batch-quickstart
- [problem] On Google models, every request in a batch must use the same response_format; mismatched formats cause validation to fail and name the first conflicting request. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/batch-quickstart
- [fact] The only supported completion window for batches is 24h. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/batch-quickstart
- [concept] Polling uses the batch ID to retrieve status, which progresses through validating, running, and then a terminal state like completed, failed, expired, or cancelled. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/batch-quickstart
- [fact] When a batch is in progress or has failed/expired/cancelled, the results field is null; results are returned inline as an array only when the batch completes. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/batch-quickstart
- [fact] Each result maps back to an input using custom_id, with exactly one of response or error populated for each item. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/batch-quickstart
- [actionable] To flag a bad generation, copy the response.body.id (e.g., gen-batch-...) and submit it via Report Feedback using the By generation ID flow. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/batch-quickstart
- [concept] The top-level endpoint determines the request shape for all items in a batch; supported shapes are /v1/chat/completions, /v1/responses, and /v1/messages. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/batch-quickstart
- [idea] To mix API shapes, submit separate batches rather than attempting to combine them in a single request. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/batch-quickstart
- [fact] OpenRouter stores batch inputs and results as JSONL artifacts in Google Cloud Storage and deletes them 30 days after creation. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/batch-quickstart
- [idea] Download any batch results before the 30-day retention window elapses to prevent data loss. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/batch-quickstart

- [definition] Conversation state and message formats — Conversation helpers and message format converters are available from the package barrel: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/agent-migration#conversation-state-and-message-formats

- [definition] Automated migration — The script below handles **subpath imports** automatically. - [definition] Can I use both packages together? — Yes. They are designed to work side by side. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/agent-migration#can-i-use-both-packages-together
- [definition] Will the old imports keep working? — The agent exports will be removed from `@openrouter/sdk` in a future major version. Update your imports now to avoid a breaking change later. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/agent-migration#will-the-old-imports-keep-working
- [definition] Do I need to change my API key or configuration? — No. `@openrouter/agent` uses the same API key and endpoints. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/agent-migration#do-i-need-to-change-my-api-key-or-configuration

- [definition] Create — Create a new bring-your-own-key (BYOK) provider credential. The raw key is encrypted at rest and never returned in API responses. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/go/sdks/byok/README#create
- [definition] Delete — Delete (soft-delete) a bring-your-own-key (BYOK) provider credential by its `id`. The encrypted key material is wiped and the record is marked as deleted. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/go/sdks/byok/README#delete
- [definition] Get — Get a single bring-your-own-key (BYOK) provider credential by its `id`. [Management key](/docs/client-sdks/go/docs/guides/overview/auth/management-api-keys) required. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/go/sdks/byok/README#get
- [definition] Update — Update an existing bring-your-own-key (BYOK) provider credential by its `id`. Include the `key` field to rotate the raw provider API key in-place (the previous key material is overwritten). — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/go/sdks/byok/README#update
- [concept] BYOK endpoints allow listing, creating, deleting, getting, and updating bring-your-own-key provider credentials. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/go/sdks/byok/README
- [fact] The raw key is encrypted at rest and never returned in API responses after creation. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/go/sdks/byok/README
- [problem] If the default workspace has been deleted, omitting `workspace_id` during creation returns a 400 error requiring explicit specification. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/go/sdks/byok/README
- [fact] The raw key is treated as write-only and is never returned after the initial creation request. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/go/sdks/byok/README
- [actionable] Use the `allowed_api_key_hashes` parameter to restrict a credential to specific OpenRouter API keys. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/go/sdks/byok/README
- [fact] The List operation scopes results to the authenticated entity's default workspace unless `workspace_id` or `provider` query parameters are used. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/go/sdks/byok/README
- [fact] The Delete operation performs a soft-delete, wiping encrypted key material and marking the record as deleted. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/go/sdks/byok/README
- [actionable] Include the `key` field in an Update request to rotate the raw provider API key in-place, overwriting previous material. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/go/sdks/byok/README
- [fact] Setting `allowed_api_key_hashes` to `null` during an Update clears the restriction on specific OpenRouter API keys. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/go/sdks/byok/README
- [fact] All BYOK operations require a Management key for authentication. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/go/sdks/byok/README
- [concept] The List operation can filter results by upstream provider using the `provider` query parameter. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/go/sdks/byok/README
- [fact] The Get operation retrieves a single BYOK provider credential identified by its `id`. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/go/sdks/byok/README
- [fact] The Update operation modifies an existing credential by its `id`. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/go/sdks/byok/README
