- [definition] GetAppRankings — Returns the top public apps on OpenRouter ranked by token usage inside the requested date window, matching the public apps marketplace on openrouter.ai/apps. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/go/sdks/datasets/README#getapprankings
- [definition] GetRankingsDaily — Returns the top 50 public models per day by total token usage on OpenRouter, plus a single aggregated `other` row per day that sums every model outside that top 50. Token totals are `prompt_tokens + completion_tokens`, matching the public rankings chart on openrouter.ai/rankings. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/go/sdks/datasets/README#getrankingsdaily
- [definition] GetSessionCost — Returns weekly refreshed, aggregated cost-per-session cells for the published harnesses. Sessions are never pooled across apps. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/go/sdks/datasets/README#getsessioncost

- [fact] Token totals for GetAppRankings are calculated as prompt_tokens plus completion_tokens, excluding hidden and private apps. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/go/sdks/datasets/README
- [concept] The sort=popular parameter ranks apps by total token volume inside the requested date window. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/go/sdks/datasets/README
- [concept] The sort=trending parameter ranks apps by absolute excess token growth, omitting apps with no excess growth. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/go/sdks/datasets/README
- [fact] When using the offset parameter for pagination, the rank value remains absolute rather than resetting. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/go/sdks/datasets/README
- [problem] Token counts from different upstream providers use their own tokenizers, making tokens attributed to one app not directly comparable to another. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/go/sdks/datasets/README
- [fact] GetAppRankings is rate-limited to 30 requests per minute per key and 500 requests per day per account. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/go/sdks/datasets/README
- [idea] When republishing or quoting the dataset, OpenRouter must be cited as 'Source: OpenRouter (openrouter.ai/apps), as of {as_of}.' — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/go/sdks/datasets/README
- [concept] GetRankingsDaily returns the top 50 public models per day plus a single aggregated 'other' row for all remaining models. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/go/sdks/datasets/README
- [fact] The 'other' row uses the reserved permaslug 'other' and is always returned last within its date group. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/go/sdks/datasets/README
- [problem] Filters for category and language_type cannot be combined with each other or with exact filters like modality, and they reject period=day with a 400 error. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/go/sdks/datasets/README
- [fact] GetRankingsDaily supports period filters of day, week, or month to set the time grain of the results. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/go/sdks/datasets/README
- [concept] GetSessionCost returns weekly refreshed, aggregated cost-per-session cells for published harnesses without pooling sessions across apps. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/go/sdks/datasets/README
- [fact] Privacy-preserving aggregation in GetSessionCost never exposes clerk_user_id values or individual per-session rows. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/go/sdks/datasets/README
- [idea] Filtering by model alone in GetSessionCost allows for harness-vs-harness comparison at a fixed model across different apps. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/go/sdks/datasets/README
- [fact] GetSessionCost results include the source snapshot window in the meta field. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/go/sdks/datasets/README

- [definition] List — Lists files belonging to the workspace of the authenticating API key. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/go/sdks/files/README#list
- [definition] Upload — Uploads a file to be referenced in future API calls. The file is stored under the workspace of the authenticating API key. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/go/sdks/files/README#upload
- [definition] Delete — Deletes a file owned by the requesting workspace. Deletion is irreversible. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/go/sdks/files/README#delete
- [definition] Retrieve — Retrieves metadata for a single file owned by the requesting workspace. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/go/sdks/files/README#retrieve

- [fact] The maximum file size allowed for upload is 100 MB, and empty files are rejected. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/go/sdks/files/README
- [concept] File type detection is determined from the file contents rather than the filename or declared content type. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/go/sdks/files/README
- [fact] Supported file types include PDF, PNG/JPEG/GIF/WebP images, DOCX/XLSX/PPTX documents, MP3/WAV/FLAC/OGG audio files, and UTF-8 text. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/go/sdks/files/README
- [fact] Text files are reported with specific MIME types such as application/json, application/x-ndjson, text/csv, text/markdown, or text/plain. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/go/sdks/files/README
- [problem] Uploaded files cannot be downloaded; attempting to download them returns a 400 error. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/go/sdks/files/README
- [fact] Only files created server-side are downloadable via the Download endpoint. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/go/sdks/files/README
- [problem] File deletion is irreversible once performed. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/go/sdks/files/README
- [concept] The List operation retrieves all files belonging to the workspace of the authenticating API key. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/go/sdks/files/README
- [concept] The Upload operation stores a file under the workspace of the authenticating API key for future reference. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/go/sdks/files/README
- [concept] The Retrieve operation fetches metadata for a single file owned by the requesting workspace. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/go/sdks/files/README
- [concept] The Download operation retrieves the raw bytes of a supported file. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/go/sdks/files/README
- [fact] The List endpoint returns an operations.ListFilesResponse object or an error. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/go/sdks/files/README
- [fact] The Upload and Retrieve endpoints return a components.FileResponse object or an error. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/go/sdks/files/README
- [fact] The Delete endpoint returns a components.FileDeleteResponse object or an error. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/go/sdks/files/README
- [fact] The Download endpoint returns an io.ReadCloser object or an error. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/go/sdks/files/README

- [parameter] **Use when**: Client SDKs=You want direct model calls and manage orchestration yourself; Agent SDK=You want built-in agent loops, tool execution, and state management — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/overview#client-sdks-vs-agent-sdk
- [parameter] **Conversation state**: Client SDKs=You manage it; Agent SDK=Managed for you via `callModel` — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/overview#client-sdks-vs-agent-sdk
- [parameter] **Tool execution**: Client SDKs=You dispatch tool calls; Agent SDK=Automatic with the `tool()` helper — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/overview#client-sdks-vs-agent-sdk
- [parameter] **Languages**: Client SDKs=TypeScript, Python, Go; Agent SDK=TypeScript — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/overview#client-sdks-vs-agent-sdk
- [definition] Client SDKs — Lightweight, type-safe clients for the OpenRouter API — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/overview#client-sdks
- [definition] When to use the Client SDKs — Choose the Client SDKs when you need **direct, efficient access to model inference** and want to manage your own application logic: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/overview#when-to-use-the-client-sdks

- [parameter] **Post-processing**: HITL (`onToolCalled`)=`onResponseReceived` transforms human input; `requireApproval`=Not available — https://openrouter.ai/docs/cookbook/building-agents/hitl-tools#hitl-vs-requireapproval
- [parameter] **Best for**: HITL (`onToolCalled`)=Conditional escalation, tiered approval, enrichment; `requireApproval`=Consent gates before risky actions — https://openrouter.ai/docs/cookbook/building-agents/hitl-tools#hitl-vs-requireapproval

The key hook for this use case is **Stop**, which fires every time Claude finishes a response cycle. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/cookbook/coding-agents/automatic-code-review#understanding-the-stop-hook
- [definition] How `decision: "block"` works — 1. The hook command runs and outputs JSON to stdout 2. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/cookbook/coding-agents/automatic-code-review#how-decision-block-works
- [definition] Why Async Matters — A simpler synchronous approach — running the full review inside the Stop hook — has three problems: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/cookbook/coding-agents/automatic-code-review#why-async-matters
- [definition] The Two-Command Architecture — The tool splits into two commands: **check** (the fast gate, called by the hook) and **review** (the actual work, spawned by Claude as a background task). — https://openrouter.ai/docs/cookbook/coding-agents/automatic-code-review#the-two-command-architecture
- [definition] Building the check command — The check command runs on every Stop event and must complete in under a second. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/cookbook/coding-agents/automatic-code-review#building-the-check-command
- [definition] Building the review command — The review command is spawned by Claude as a background task. It streams Codex output in real-time for progress visibility, then prints a final summary. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/cookbook/coding-agents/automatic-code-review#building-the-review-command
- [definition] The reason text that instructs Claude — The check command's `reason` field includes the diff stat and lets Claude decide whether to review: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/cookbook/coding-agents/automatic-code-review#the-reason-text-that-instructs-claude
- [definition] Installing and Removing the Hook — The tool should provide commands to programmatically install and remove the hook from `.claude/settings.local.json`. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/cookbook/coding-agents/automatic-code-review#installing-and-removing-the-hook
- [definition] Test check with no changes — Ensure your working tree is clean, then: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/cookbook/coding-agents/automatic-code-review#test-check-with-no-changes
- [definition] Full integration test — 1. Install the hook: `redline install` 2. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/cookbook/coding-agents/automatic-code-review#full-integration-test
- [definition] Claude Code only — This pattern relies on Claude Code's `decision: "block"` hook output, which injects instructions directly into the agent's conversation. Codex CLI's hook system (as of early 2026) is more limited — its `Stop` hook is fire-and-forget and cannot feed structured output back into the model's context. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/cookbook/coding-agents/automatic-code-review#claude-code-only
- [definition] Review granularity — The review covers everything uncommitted — all staged, unstaged, and untracked changes. It does not distinguish between changes Claude just made and pre-existing uncommitted work. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/cookbook/coding-agents/automatic-code-review#review-granularity

- [definition] Context length errors — Hermes requires a model with at least **64K context tokens**. - [definition] Max Effort Level — A new `'max'` effort level is available for Claude 4.6 Opus and 4.6 Sonnet via the `verbosity` parameter. - [definition] Verbosity vs Reasoning Effort — On Claude 4.6, both parameters set the same upstream value: Anthropic's `output_config.effort`. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/cookbook/evaluate-and-optimize/model-migrations/claude-4-6#verbosity-vs-reasoning-effort
- [definition] Breaking Changes — None. Existing requests continue to work: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/cookbook/evaluate-and-optimize/model-migrations/claude-4-6#breaking-changes

This field is critical for multi-turn agentic workflows — it tells the model whether an assistant message is intermediate commentary or the final answer. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/cookbook/evaluate-and-optimize/model-migrations/gpt-5-4#whats-new
- [definition] The `phase` Field — `phase` appears on assistant output messages and has three possible values: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/cookbook/evaluate-and-optimize/model-migrations/gpt-5-4#the-phase-field
- [definition] Why It Matters — For models like `gpt-5.3-codex`, `gpt-5.4`, `gpt-5.4-pro`, `gpt-5.5`, and `gpt-5.5-pro`, correctly preserving `phase` on assistant messages is **required** for optimal performance. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/cookbook/evaluate-and-optimize/model-migrations/gpt-5-4#why-it-matters
- [definition] Responses API — When using the Responses API, assistant output items include `phase`. You must persist these items verbatim and pass them back in subsequent requests. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/cookbook/evaluate-and-optimize/model-migrations/gpt-5-4#responses-api
- [definition] Chat Completions API — The Chat Completions API does **not** support `phase` in responses. A single chat completion response can only contain one message per choice, so there is no way to represent the separate commentary and final answer output items that models like GPT-5.4 produce. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/cookbook/evaluate-and-optimize/model-migrations/gpt-5-4#chat-completions-api
- [definition] Implementation Pattern — When building an integration with the Responses API, persist your output items verbatim, including `phase` on assistant messages: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/cookbook/evaluate-and-optimize/model-migrations/gpt-5-4#implementation-pattern
- [definition] Key Rules — 1. **Preserve phase on assistant messages** — When you receive a response with `phase`, store it and send it back on subsequent requests. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/cookbook/evaluate-and-optimize/model-migrations/gpt-5-4#key-rules

- [definition] How RAG Works — A typical RAG pipeline follows these steps: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/cookbook/evaluate-and-optimize/rag#how-rag-works
- [definition] Step 1: Index Your Documents — Split your documents into chunks and generate embeddings for each chunk. Store the embeddings in a vector database (or in-memory for prototyping). — https://openrouter.ai/docs/cookbook/evaluate-and-optimize/rag#step-1-index-your-documents
- [definition] Step 2: Retrieve Relevant Documents — When a user asks a question, embed the query and find the most similar document chunks using cosine similarity. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/cookbook/evaluate-and-optimize/rag#step-2-retrieve-relevant-documents
- [definition] Step 3: Rerank for Better Precision — Embedding-based retrieval is fast but approximate. A rerank model uses a cross-encoder to compare each document directly against the query, producing more accurate relevance scores. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/cookbook/evaluate-and-optimize/rag#step-3-rerank-for-better-precision
- [definition] Step 4: Generate an Answer with Context — Pass the top-ranked documents as context to a chat model. The LLM generates a grounded answer based on the retrieved information. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/cookbook/evaluate-and-optimize/rag#step-4-generate-an-answer-with-context
- [definition] Complete Example — Here is a full end-to-end RAG pipeline combining all four steps: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/cookbook/evaluate-and-optimize/rag#complete-example
- [definition] When to Use Rerank — Reranking adds an extra API call, so it's worth understanding when it helps most: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/cookbook/evaluate-and-optimize/rag#when-to-use-rerank
- [definition] Multimodal Rerank (Text + Images) — Some rerank models accept images alongside text. Instead of passing plain strings, you pass document objects with an optional `text` field, an optional `image` field, or both. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/cookbook/evaluate-and-optimize/rag#multimodal-rerank-text-images
- [definition] Chunking Strategies — How you split documents significantly affects retrieval quality: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/cookbook/evaluate-and-optimize/rag#chunking-strategies

## Red Teaming
<https://openrouter.ai/docs/cookbook/evaluate-and-optimize/red-teaming>

- [definition] Red Teaming — Policy for red teaming and adversarial testing on OpenRouter — https://openrouter.ai/docs/cookbook/evaluate-and-optimize/red-teaming#red-teaming
- [definition] Approval Required — Because most model and provider terms of service do not support red-teaming, you cannot red-team models on OpenRouter without prior approval. This includes prompt injection, jailbreaking, or any attempt to get models to behave in ways that violate their terms of service. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/cookbook/evaluate-and-optimize/red-teaming#approval-required
- [definition] Legitimate Red Teaming — OpenRouter supports legitimate AI safety research and red teaming with prior approval. Getting approval allows us to coordinate with providers and prevent your account from being flagged for policy violations. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/cookbook/evaluate-and-optimize/red-teaming#legitimate-red-teaming
- [definition] Compatibility with Zero Data Retention — Note that certain types of safety classifiers are run online (while the prompt is in-flight and in-memory). Prompts may therefore be flagged by classifiers even with full ZDR configured. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/cookbook/evaluate-and-optimize/red-teaming#compatibility-with-zero-data-retention
- [definition] Request Approval — To request red teaming approval, email [safety@openrouter.ai](mailto:safety@openrouter.ai) with the following details: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/cookbook/evaluate-and-optimize/red-teaming#request-approval

- [definition] Tuning the system prompt — The system prompt controls how aggressively the orchestrator rewrites. Some patterns: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/cookbook/image-generation/preset-enhanced-images#tuning-the-system-prompt

- [definition] Using different image models for different scenarios — The image model is fixed per preset (the orchestrator can't switch it mid-request). - [definition] Updating the preset without redeploying — One of the key benefits: change the image model, tune the system prompt, or adjust parameters from the [Presets dashboard](https://openrouter.ai/settings/presets) or via the API. No code deploy needed. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/cookbook/image-generation/preset-enhanced-images#updating-the-preset-without-redeploying

- [definition] Billing — Classifier tokens bill like any other generation against your workspace's credits. You control cost through model choice: picking a small, fast model (like Haiku or Flash) keeps classification costs low. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/classifiers#billing
- [definition] Failure Handling — If classification fails (timeout, model error, invalid output), the generation proceeds normally with no tags written. Classification failures don't affect your API responses. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/classifiers#failure-handling

- [definition] Assigning Guardrails — A guardrail enforces nothing until it is assigned. - [definition] Guardrail Hierarchy — Account-wide privacy and provider settings are always enforced as a default guardrail. When additional guardrails apply to a request, they are combined using the following rules: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/guardrails#guardrail-hierarchy
- [definition] Eligibility Preview — When viewing a guardrail, you can see an eligibility preview that shows which providers and models are available with that guardrail combined with your account settings. This helps you understand the effective restrictions before assigning the guardrail. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/guardrails#eligibility-preview
- [definition] Budget Enforcement — Guardrail budgets are enforced per-user and per-key, not shared across all users with that guardrail. When an API key makes a request, its usage counts toward both the key's budget and the owning member's budget. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/guardrails#budget-enforcement
- [definition] Custom Content Filters — Each guardrail can carry a list of **custom content filter patterns**. Every pattern is a regular expression with an associated action: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/guardrails#custom-content-filters
- [definition] Supported regex features — Patterns are JavaScript-flavoured regular expressions. The following common constructs are all supported: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/guardrails#supported-regex-features
- [definition] Unsupported regex features — To keep evaluation fast and predictable across all requests, the following features are **not allowed** in new or edited patterns: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/guardrails#unsupported-regex-features
- [definition] When a Request Is Blocked — When a guardrail's runtime checks block a request (for example a content filter or prompt-injection detector), OpenRouter returns an HTTP **403 Forbidden** response. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/guardrails#when-a-request-is-blocked
- [definition] API Access — You can manage guardrails programmatically using the OpenRouter API. This allows you to create, update, delete, and assign guardrails to API keys and organization members directly from your code. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/guardrails#api-access
- [definition] Updating the Workspace Default Guardrail via API — Each workspace has a **default guardrail** that applies to all traffic in that workspace without needing to be explicitly assigned to individual keys or members. To update the workspace default guardrail via the API: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/guardrails#updating-the-workspace-default-guardrail-via-api

## Prompt Injection Detection
<https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/guardrails/prompt-injection>

- [definition] Prompt Injection Detection — Regex-based prompt injection guardrail patterns — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/guardrails/prompt-injection#prompt-injection-detection
- [definition] How It Works — When regex-based detection is enabled on a guardrail, every incoming message is scanned against a set of patterns derived from the [OWASP LLM Prompt Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/LLM_Prompt_Injection_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html), among other… — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/guardrails/prompt-injection#how-it-works
- [definition] Detection Patterns — The following regex patterns are checked against all user-supplied message content. Patterns are case-insensitive unless noted otherwise. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/guardrails/prompt-injection#detection-patterns
- [definition] Evasion Detection — In addition to the regex patterns above, the detection system includes techniques to catch common evasion strategies. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/guardrails/prompt-injection#evasion-detection
- [definition] Typoglycemia Detection — Attackers may scramble the middle letters of keywords while keeping the first and last letters intact (e.g., "ignroe" instead of "ignore"). The system checks for typoglycemia variants of these target words: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/guardrails/prompt-injection#typoglycemia-detection
- [definition] Encoding-Based Evasion — The system decodes Base64 and hex-encoded content (including space-separated hex pairs like `69 67 6e 6f 72 65`), then checks the decoded text for injection keywords: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/guardrails/prompt-injection#encoding-based-evasion
- [definition] Character-Spaced Evasion — Text with character spacing (e.g., `i g n o r e  p r e v i o u s`) is normalized by collapsing spaces, then re-scanned against all patterns. This prevents simple spacing-based evasion. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/guardrails/prompt-injection#character-spaced-evasion
- [definition] Reporting False Positives — If a detection incorrectly flags legitimate content, you can mark it as a false positive from the [Logs](https://openrouter.ai/logs) page. Generations with a guardrail event show a shield icon on the row; hover it to open the guardrail popover. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/guardrails/prompt-injection#reporting-false-positives

## Allowlist
<https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/guardrails/prompt-injection/allowlist>

- [definition] Allowlist — Exclude known-safe phrases from prompt injection detection — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/guardrails/prompt-injection/allowlist#allowlist
- [definition] How It Works — When a request is scanned for prompt injection, allowlisted phrases are masked before the detection patterns run: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/guardrails/prompt-injection/allowlist#how-it-works
- [definition] Managing Patterns — Allowlist patterns are managed per-user from [Settings > Privacy](https://openrouter.ai/settings/privacy). Your allowlist applies across every guardrail that scans your requests — unlike detection configuration, which is set per-guardrail, the allowlist is entity-scoped. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/guardrails/prompt-injection/allowlist#managing-patterns
- [definition] Adding a Pattern — Click **Add pattern** and enter the phrase you want to allowlist. A live character counter shows the current length against the 1,000-character limit. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/guardrails/prompt-injection/allowlist#adding-a-pattern
- [definition] Editing a Pattern — Click the pencil icon on an existing pattern to open the inline edit form. The system checks for duplicate patterns (case-insensitive) before saving — if an identical pattern already exists, the edit is rejected with a toast notification. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/guardrails/prompt-injection/allowlist#editing-a-pattern
- [definition] Toggling Active / Inactive — Each pattern has a toggle switch. Inactive patterns are visually dimmed and are not applied during detection. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/guardrails/prompt-injection/allowlist#toggling-active-inactive
- [definition] Deleting a Pattern — Click the trash icon on a pattern to permanently remove it. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/guardrails/prompt-injection/allowlist#deleting-a-pattern
- [definition] Quick-Add from Activity — When reviewing guardrail events in the [Logs](https://openrouter.ai/logs) prompt detail view, prompt injection events display an **Add to allowlist** banner that lets you add detected phrases directly to your allowlist without navigating to Settings. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/guardrails/prompt-injection/allowlist#quick-add-from-activity

- [definition] Sensitive Info Guardrail — Automatically detect and handle sensitive information in API requests — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/guardrails/sensitive-info#sensitive-info-guardrail
- [definition] How It Works — When a Sensitive Info Guardrail is active, every API request is scanned before it is forwarded to the model provider: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/guardrails/sensitive-info#how-it-works
- [definition] Detection Methods — OpenRouter uses two complementary detection methods: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/guardrails/sensitive-info#detection-methods
- [definition] Regex-Based Detection — Most built-in presets and all custom patterns use regular expression matching. This is fast, deterministic, and adds negligible latency to requests. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/guardrails/sensitive-info#regex-based-detection
- [definition] NLP-Based Detection — Some types of sensitive information — like person names and geographic locations — cannot be reliably detected with simple patterns. For these, OpenRouter uses NLP-powered entity recognition (via [Presidio](https://microsoft.github.io/presidio/)), which analyzes text contextually. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/guardrails/sensitive-info#nlp-based-detection
- [definition] Built-In Presets — The following presets are available out of the box. Each can be individually enabled and configured with either the **Redact** or **Block** action. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/guardrails/sensitive-info#built-in-presets
- [definition] Secrets Preset — The **Secrets** preset detects well-known provider-prefixed API keys and credential formats with low false-positive rates. By default, matches are redacted as `[SECRET:<format-id>]`, such as `[SECRET:github-token]`. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/guardrails/sensitive-info#secrets-preset
- [definition] NLP Preset Limitations — NLP-based detection is contextual and probabilistic. Keep the following in mind: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/guardrails/sensitive-info#nlp-preset-limitations
- [definition] Custom Patterns — In addition to built-in presets, you can define your own custom regex patterns to detect domain-specific sensitive information. Each custom pattern requires: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/guardrails/sensitive-info#custom-patterns
- [definition] Via the Dashboard — 1. Navigate to your workspace's **Privacy & Guardrails** page, or go to [Settings > Privacy](https://openrouter.ai/settings/privacy). — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/guardrails/sensitive-info#via-the-dashboard
- [definition] Via the API — Sensitive info filters are configured as part of the guardrail object using the `content_filter_builtins` and `content_filters` fields. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/guardrails/sensitive-info#via-the-api
- [definition] How Sensitive Info Interacts with Other Guardrails — Sensitive info filters follow the same [guardrail hierarchy](/docs/guides/features/guardrails#guardrail-hierarchy) as other guardrail settings. When multiple guardrails apply to a request: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/guardrails/sensitive-info#how-sensitive-info-interacts-with-other-guardrails
- [definition] Error Responses — When a request is blocked by a content filter, the API returns: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/guardrails/sensitive-info#error-responses
- [definition] Reporting False Positives — If a detection incorrectly flags legitimate content, you can mark it as a false positive from the [Logs](https://openrouter.ai/logs) page. Generations with a guardrail event show a shield icon on the row; hover it to open the guardrail popover. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/guardrails/sensitive-info#reporting-false-positives

- [definition] Filtering by API Key — By default, Input & Output Logging applies to requests from all of your API keys. In the **API Keys Filter** section of your Observability settings, you can narrow this down: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/input-output-logging#filtering-by-api-key
- [definition] Viewing Stored Prompts — Once Input & Output Logging is enabled, you can view your stored prompts and completions from the [Logs](https://openrouter.ai/logs) page: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/input-output-logging#viewing-stored-prompts
- [definition] Regional routing limitation — At this time, Input & Output Logging does **not** apply to requests routed through `eu.openrouter.ai` or `us.openrouter.ai`. If you have in-region routing enabled, requests processed through either regional endpoint will work as normal but input/output logging will be skipped. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/input-output-logging#regional-routing-limitation
- [definition] Comparison with Broadcast — Input & Output Logging allows you to view your prompts and completions in your logs on the OpenRouter platform. Broadcast sends your data to an external observability tool. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/input-output-logging#comparison-with-broadcast
- [definition] Comparison with OpenRouter Using Inputs/Outputs — Input & Output Logging keeps your data strictly private for your own use, makes your prompts and completions visible in logs, and is enabled in Observability. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/input-output-logging#comparison-with-openrouter-using-inputsoutputs

- [definition] Response Caching — Cache responses for identical API requests to save time and money — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/response-caching#response-caching
- [definition] Enabling caching — There are two ways to enable response caching: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/response-caching#enabling-caching
- [definition] 1. Per-request via headers — Add the `X-OpenRouter-Cache` header to enable caching for individual requests: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/response-caching#1-per-request-via-headers
- [definition] 2. Via presets — You can enable caching for all requests that use a specific [preset](/docs/guides/features/presets) by configuring these fields in the preset: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/response-caching#2-via-presets
- [definition] How it works — Two requests are considered identical when they share the same API key, model, endpoint type, streaming mode, and request body (including all parameters). When caching is enabled, OpenRouter generates a cache key from these inputs. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/response-caching#how-it-works
- [definition] Cache key details — The cache key is derived from your **API key**, **model**, **endpoint type**, **streaming mode**, and a **SHA-256 hash of the request body**. Streaming and non-streaming requests are cached separately, so a `stream: true` request will not return a cached non-streaming response and vice versa. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/response-caching#cache-key-details
- [definition] Precedence — Request headers and [preset](/docs/guides/features/presets) configuration interact as follows: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/response-caching#precedence
- [definition] Concurrent requests — If two identical requests arrive simultaneously before the first response is written to cache, both result in a cache `MISS` and are billed independently. There is no request coalescing. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/response-caching#concurrent-requests
- [definition] TTL (Time-to-Live) — The TTL controls how long a cached response remains valid. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/response-caching#ttl-time-to-live
- [definition] Cache clearing — To force a fresh response for a specific request, send the `X-OpenRouter-Cache-Clear: true` header alongside `X-OpenRouter-Cache: true` (or with a preset that has `cache_enabled: true`). — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/response-caching#cache-clearing
- [definition] Billing — Cache hits are **free**. No tokens are consumed and all billable usage counters are reported as `0`. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/response-caching#billing
- [definition] Data retention — Cached responses are stored in edge infrastructure, retained only for the TTL duration, and automatically evicted upon expiry. Cached data is accessible only via the API key that triggered the caching–no other key, account, or organization can retrieve it. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/response-caching#data-retention
- [definition] Agent workflows — When an agent workflow fails partway through, you can resume from the point of failure without re-running and re-paying for identical earlier requests. Enable caching at the start of the workflow and all prior steps return immediately from cache on retry. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/response-caching#agent-workflows
- [definition] Unit testing — Get repeatable responses for your test suite. After the initial run populates the cache, subsequent identical requests return the same cached response every time at zero cost. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/response-caching#unit-testing
- [definition] Repeated identical requests — If your application makes the same request multiple times (same model, same messages, same parameters), caching ensures only the first call hits the provider. Subsequent identical calls return immediately from cache at zero cost. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/response-caching#repeated-identical-requests
- [definition] Monitoring cache effectiveness — Cache hit and miss status is visible in your [Activity log](https://openrouter.ai/logs). Each cached request appears as a separate entry with a cache indicator, and you can filter the log to show only cached or non-cached requests. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/response-caching#monitoring-cache-effectiveness

- [parameter] `engine`: Type=string; Default=`auto`; Description=`auto`: uses native passthrough when the endpoint supports incremental diff streaming, otherwise falls back to OpenRouter's HITL validator. `native`: forces native passthrough (falls back to HITL if unsupported). `openrouter`: always uses the HITL validator, even on endpoints with native support. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/apply-patch#configuration
- [definition] Apply Patch — Let models propose file changes via V4A diffs — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/apply-patch#apply-patch
- [definition] How It Works — 1. You include `{ "type": "openrouter:apply_patch" }` in your `tools` array when calling the Responses API. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/apply-patch#how-it-works
- [definition] Patch Operations — The tool supports three operation types, each carried as the `operation` field on the `apply_patch_call` output item: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/apply-patch#patch-operations
- [definition] `create_file` — Creates a new file. Every content line in the diff must start with `+`: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/apply-patch#create-file
- [definition] `update_file` — Updates an existing file using a V4A diff with context lines (` ` prefix), additions (`+`), and deletions (`-`): — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/apply-patch#update-file
- [definition] `delete_file` — Deletes a file. No diff is needed, only the file path: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/apply-patch#delete-file
- [definition] Echoing Results — After your application applies (or rejects) the patch, send the result back on the next turn as an `apply_patch_call_output` input item: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/apply-patch#echoing-results
- [definition] Configuration — The apply patch tool accepts an optional `engine` parameter: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/apply-patch#configuration
- [definition] Pricing — The apply patch tool has no additional cost beyond standard token usage. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/apply-patch#pricing

- [parameter] `analysis_models`: Default=Quality preset (`~anthropic/claude-opus-latest`, `~openai/gpt-latest`, `~google/gemini-pro-latest`); Description=Models that form the panel. Each runs in parallel with `openrouter:web_search` and `openrouter:web_fetch` enabled. 1–8 models allowed. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/fusion#parameters
- [parameter] `model`: Default=Your outer model; Description=The analyst that produces the structured analysis JSON. Defaults to the same model handling your request. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/fusion#parameters
- [parameter] `max_tool_calls`: Default=`4`; Description=Max tool-calling steps each panel model and the analyst may take in their `openrouter:web_search` / `openrouter:web_fetch` loop before they must return text. Range 1–16. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/fusion#parameters
- [parameter] `max_completion_tokens`: Default=`16000`; Description=Max output tokens (including reasoning) per inner panel/analyst call. Keeps reasoning-heavy models from exhausting their budget before producing visible text. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/fusion#parameters
- [parameter] `reasoning`: Default=Provider default; Description=Reasoning config forwarded to the panel and analyst calls: an object with optional `effort` and `max_tokens`. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/fusion#parameters
- [parameter] `temperature`: Default=Provider default; Description=Temperature (`0`–`2`) forwarded to the panel calls. The analyst always runs at temperature 0. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/fusion#parameters
- [parameter] `all_panels_failed`: Every panel model returned an error. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/fusion#hard-failures
- [parameter] `insufficient_credits`: Every panel model failed and at least one was due to insufficient credits. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/fusion#hard-failures
- [parameter] `rate_limited`: Every panel model failed and at least one was rate-limited. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/fusion#hard-failures
- [parameter] `fusion_invocation_capped`: Fusion was already invoked earlier in the same turn; a second call is rejected. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/fusion#hard-failures
- [parameter] `unexpected_error`: An unexpected error interrupted the fusion run. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/fusion#hard-failures
- [definition] Fusion — Multi-model deliberation as a server tool — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/fusion#fusion
- [definition] When does the model invoke it? — The tool's description tells the model to call `openrouter:fusion` only when a task genuinely benefits from multiple perspectives: research questions, multi-domain critique, "compare and contrast" prompts, or anything where being wrong is expensive. Simple tactical prompts won't trigger it. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/fusion#when-does-the-model-invoke-it
- [definition] Parameters — Pass an optional `parameters` object on the tool entry to override defaults: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/fusion#parameters
- [definition] What the tool returns — On success, the tool result contains the structured analysis and the raw panel responses: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/fusion#what-the-tool-returns
- [definition] Analyst degradation — If the **panel** succeeds but the **analyst** fails (an upstream error, an empty completion, or output that isn't valid analysis JSON), the tool does **not** error. It returns `status: "ok"` with the raw panel `responses` and simply **omits** `analysis`. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/fusion#analyst-degradation
- [definition] Hard failures — The tool only returns `status: "error"` when it can't produce any useful output. In that case it includes a typed `failure_reason`: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/fusion#hard-failures
- [definition] Web tools — `openrouter:web_search` and `openrouter:web_fetch` are enabled on both the **panel** and the **analyst** calls, so models can pull fresh sources while they answer and analyze. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/fusion#web-tools
- [definition] Recursion protection — Inner fusion calls carry an `x-openrouter-fusion-depth` header. Panel and analyst models cannot recursively invoke `openrouter:fusion`. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/fusion#recursion-protection

- [definition] OpenAI native shell tool — On the Responses API you can also send OpenAI's native tool shape (`{ "type": "shell" }`, or the legacy Codex `local_shell`) instead of `openrouter:shell`. On OpenAI models this uses OpenAI's own hosted shell; on any other model, OpenRouter routes the call to its sandbox transparently. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/shell#openai-native-shell-tool
- [definition] Response Format — The tool returns one entry per command, matching OpenAI's `shell_call_output.output[]`: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/shell#response-format

- [definition] Worker tools — When you pass `tools`, the worker runs as an agentic sub-agent over them before producing its outcome. For example, giving the worker `openrouter:web_search` lets it ground its result in fresh sources. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/subagent#worker-tools
- [definition] What happens when a subagent calls a local tool — When the subagent calls an inherited client tool, its run pauses and the response's turn ends (it is possible for the subagent to also call multiple tools in parallel). The response output contains: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/subagent#what-happens-when-a-subagent-calls-a-local-tool
- [definition] Replaying to resume the worker — To preserve subagent state when returning the output of `function_call` items, you must send the conversation back: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/subagent#replaying-to-resume-the-worker
- [definition] Streaming — With `stream: true`, the suspension surfaces through the standard Responses SSE events with one contract worth knowing: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/subagent#streaming
- [definition] Failure handling — A failed worker never fails the response. In every failure case below, the affected worker degrades to a `status: "error"` tool result; the delegating model sees the error and continues: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/subagent#failure-handling
- [definition] Recursion protection — The subagent tool cannot invoke itself. Two guards enforce this: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/subagent#recursion-protection

## Tool Search
<https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/tool-search>

- [snippet] title="Request" expandable: { — `{` — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/tool-search#quick-start
- [parameter] Responses: `openrouter:tool_search`, `tool_search` — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/tool-search#supported-apis
- [parameter] Messages: `openrouter:tool_search`, `tool_search_tool_regex`, `tool_search_tool_regex_20251119` — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/tool-search#supported-apis
- [parameter] `max_results`: Default=`5`; Description=Maximum tools returned by a single search. The model may request fewer. Capped at 50. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/tool-search#configuration
- [definition] Tool Search — Let the model discover tools on demand instead of loading every definition up front — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/tool-search#tool-search
- [definition] Quick Start — Include the tool alongside your own, and mark the ones to withhold: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/tool-search#quick-start
- [definition] Marking Tools as Deferred — Add `defer_loading: true` to any tool you want withheld. Deferred tools are hidden by default: the model cannot see or call one until a search returns it. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/tool-search#marking-tools-as-deferred
- [definition] Searching — The model supplies a regular expression, matched case-insensitively against each deferred tool's name, description, argument names, and argument descriptions. A pattern of `weather` finds a tool whose only mention of weather is in a parameter description. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/tool-search#searching
- [definition] Controlling Tool Choice — Tool search uses `tool_choice` to express which tools the model may call on each turn, widening it as tools are discovered. OpenRouter sets this up for you. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/tool-search#controlling-tool-choice
- [definition] Prompt Caching — Discovering a tool does not disturb the tools already in the conversation, so prompt caching is preserved across a search. You can start a conversation with a small loaded set, let the model discover more as it goes, and keep your cache hit across every turn. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/tool-search#prompt-caching
- [definition] Supported APIs — Tool search is available through the [Responses API](/docs/api_reference/responses/overview) and the [Messages API](/docs/api/api-reference/anthropic-messages/create-a-message). Requesting it on the Chat Completions API returns a `400` error. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/tool-search#supported-apis
- [definition] When to Use It — Reach for tool search when your definitions exceed roughly 10k tokens, when you have more than about 10 tools, or when tool selection accuracy drops as the library grows. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/tool-search#when-to-use-it

- [parameter] `:nitro` variant: Eligible pool=Default + priority endpoints; Ordering=Entire pool sorted by throughput, no tier preference; Fallback=Next-fastest endpoint of any tier — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/service-tiers#comparing-tier-selection-options
- [parameter] `:floor` variant: Eligible pool=Default + flex endpoints; Ordering=Entire pool sorted by price, no tier preference; Fallback=Next-cheapest endpoint of any tier — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/service-tiers#comparing-tier-selection-options
- [parameter] `service_tier: "priority"` (or `"fast"`): Eligible pool=Default + priority endpoints; Ordering=Priority endpoints first, each group sorted by throughput; Fallback=Falls back to non-priority endpoints — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/service-tiers#comparing-tier-selection-options
- [parameter] `service_tier: "flex"`: Eligible pool=Flex endpoints only (when any exist); Ordering=Sorted by price; Fallback=No fallback to default endpoints, capacity errors surface — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/service-tiers#comparing-tier-selection-options
- [parameter] `provider.only` with a tier slug: Eligible pool=Only the endpoints the slugs name (tier slugs opt in that tier); Ordering=Default load-balanced ordering unless a sort is set; Fallback=Within the named endpoints only — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/service-tiers#comparing-tier-selection-options
- [parameter] `provider.order` with a tier slug: Eligible pool=Unchanged (tier slugs opt in the named tier endpoints); Ordering=Listed endpoints first, in your order; Fallback=Falls back to unlisted endpoints unless disabled — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/service-tiers#comparing-tier-selection-options
- [parameter] `provider.sort` (`"throughput"` / `"price"`): Eligible pool=Unchanged (does not opt into any tier); Ordering=Entire pool sorted by the chosen metric; Fallback=Next endpoint in sorted order — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/service-tiers#comparing-tier-selection-options
- [definition] Service Tiers — Control cost and latency tradeoffs with service tier selection — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/service-tiers#service-tiers
- [definition] Service Tiers — Many providers sell more than one grade of capacity for the same model: a discounted `flex` tier that trades latency and availability for a lower price, and a `priority` tier that costs more for faster, more reliable service. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/service-tiers#service-tiers
- [definition] The `:nitro` and `:floor` Variants — The simplest way to use service tiers is to append a variant to the model ID. `:nitro` sorts every endpoint for the model by throughput and admits priority tier endpoints into that sort. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/service-tiers#the-nitro-and-floor-variants
- [definition] Using Service Tiers — To pin a tier explicitly, pass `service_tier` as a top-level parameter in your request body. Supported values are `flex` (lower cost, higher latency) and `priority` (faster, higher cost). — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/service-tiers#using-service-tiers
- [definition] Fast mode — `service_tier: "fast"` (OpenAI's [Fast mode](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/fast-mode) rename of priority processing), `service_tier: "priority"`, and Anthropic's native `speed: "fast"` parameter are fully interchangeable on all APIs and providers. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/service-tiers#fast-mode
- [definition] How Routing Works — Non-default tier endpoints (`flex`, `priority`) are only considered when your request asks for them. There are three ways to do that: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/service-tiers#how-routing-works
- [definition] Tier Endpoints in the API — Tier endpoints are listed in the [model endpoints API](/docs/api/api-reference/endpoints/list-all-endpoints-for-a-model) alongside standard endpoints. Each appears as its own entry with a tier-suffixed `tag` (e.g. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/service-tiers#tier-endpoints-in-the-api
- [definition] Supported Providers — The following providers support `flex` and `priority` service tiers for select models: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/service-tiers#supported-providers
- [definition] API Response Differences — The API response includes a `service_tier` field that indicates which capacity tier was actually used to serve your request. The placement of this field varies by API format: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/service-tiers#api-response-differences

- [definition] Sovereign AI — Keep AI workloads within national and regional boundaries — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/sovereign-ai#sovereign-ai
- [definition] Drivers of sovereign AI — Sovereign AI is driven by two converging forces: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/sovereign-ai#drivers-of-sovereign-ai
- [definition] Regulatory Compliance — Regulations like the EU AI Act, GDPR, and sector-specific rules (healthcare, finance, defense) impose strict requirements on where data can be processed and stored. Organizations operating across jurisdictions need infrastructure that respects these boundaries. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/sovereign-ai#regulatory-compliance
- [definition] Data Residency and Privacy — Sensitive data (whether personal, financial, or classified) may not legally or ethically leave a particular jurisdiction. Sovereign AI ensures that prompts and completions are processed entirely within a designated region, with no cross-border data transfers. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/sovereign-ai#data-residency-and-privacy
- [definition] How OpenRouter Enables Sovereign AI — OpenRouter provides several features that enable sovereign AI deployments today, allowing enterprises to maintain control over where their AI workloads are processed. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/sovereign-ai#how-openrouter-enables-sovereign-ai
- [definition] In-Region Routing — For enterprise customers, OpenRouter supports in-region routing in the EU and the US. When enabled, your requests are guaranteed to only be decrypted within the designated region, and are only routed to providers operating in that region. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/sovereign-ai#in-region-routing
- [definition] Zero Data Retention (ZDR) — [Zero Data Retention](/docs/guides/features/zdr) ensures that providers do not store your prompts or responses. This is a key component of sovereign AI, as it guarantees that no data persists outside your control after a request completes. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/sovereign-ai#zero-data-retention-zdr
- [definition] Data Collection Controls — Control whether providers can collect your data with the `data_collection` parameter: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/sovereign-ai#data-collection-controls
- [definition] Building a Sovereign AI Stack with OpenRouter — Combining these features, you can build a fully sovereign AI deployment: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/sovereign-ai#building-a-sovereign-ai-stack-with-openrouter
- [definition] Getting Started — Sovereign AI features are available to all OpenRouter users, with in-region routing (EU or US) available for enterprise customers. To get started: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/sovereign-ai#getting-started

- [definition] How It Works — Zero completion insurance automatically applies to all requests across all models and providers. - [definition] What Is Covered — Zero completion insurance covers the model's inference cost: prompt tokens, completion tokens, and reasoning tokens are not billed when a response qualifies. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/zero-completion-insurance#what-is-covered
- [definition] Viewing Protected Requests — On your activity page, requests that were protected by zero completion insurance will show zero credits deducted for token usage. - [definition] Ori Eval — Find the best model for your project by testing your agent on real prompts, with one harness and one model for each run — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/ori/eval#ori-eval
- [definition] Start with your coding agent — You do not need to install or run Ori yourself. Give this instruction to your coding agent: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/ori/eval#start-with-your-coding-agent
- [definition] Why you run evals with Ori — A stable test bench is the difficult part of an eval. Ori is a harness, and not only a skill. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/ori/eval#why-you-run-evals-with-ori
- [definition] Run the steps manually — The steps below do the same work by hand. Use them when you want more control, or when you want to see what the agent wrote. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/ori/eval#run-the-steps-manually
- [definition] Start with a question — Go to your project directory, then ask Ori to make the eval: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/ori/eval#start-with-a-question
- [definition] The eval file — Read this section when you want to write an eval yourself, or when you want to see what the agent wrote. An eval file looks like a normal `bun test` file: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/ori/eval#the-eval-file
- [definition] Compare models — Get the candidate models from the live catalog of OpenRouter instead of a list of slugs that you write yourself. Set a maximum price, then run the same eval with each model: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/ori/eval#compare-models
- [definition] Give a score to an open answer — Some questions do not have one correct answer. Use an LLM judge to give a score to the answer. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/ori/eval#give-a-score-to-an-open-answer
- [definition] Use your own data — Real data from your users is better than prompts that you invent. Use `test.each` for chat logs, or for pairs of a question and an answer: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/ori/eval#use-your-own-data
- [definition] Run an eval in CI — An eval sends requests to real models, and therefore costs money. Put your evals in a separate job. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/ori/eval#run-an-eval-in-ci
- [definition] GitHub Actions — Ori needs Bun in CI. When `CI` is true, `ori eval` does not install Bun for you. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/ori/eval#github-actions

- [snippet] Any agent, any model: ori claude --model anthropic/claude-sonnet-4.6 — `ori claude --model anthropic/claude-sonnet-4.6` — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/ori/harness#any-agent-any-model
- [snippet] Any agent, any model: ori codex --model google/gemini-3.6-flash --full-auto — `ori codex --model google/gemini-3.6-flash --full-auto` — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/ori/harness#any-agent-any-model
- [definition] Ori Harness — Run your existing agent CLI on OpenRouter with any model, organization guardrails, and one bill — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/ori/harness#ori-harness
- [definition] Let your coding agent set it up — You don't need to run the setup yourself. Give this instruction to the coding agent you already use: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/ori/harness#let-your-coding-agent-set-it-up
- [definition] Bring your own agent — Run Claude Code, Codex, Grok Build, Hermes, OpenCode, Pi, Prime Agent, or DeepSeek Harness with commands you already know: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/ori/harness#bring-your-own-agent
- [definition] DeepSeek Harness — DeepSeek Harness (dsh) doesn't start and stop like the other CLIs, so Ori sets it up instead of starting it: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/ori/harness#deepseek-harness
- [definition] Sign in instead of managing keys — Run an agent and Ori opens a browser so you can sign in with your OpenRouter account. It uses OAuth PKCE, so there's no new account and no key to create or paste. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/ori/harness#sign-in-instead-of-managing-keys
- [definition] Any agent, any model — Pass `--model` and any OpenRouter model ID: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/ori/harness#any-agent-any-model
- [definition] Live model catalog and routing toggles — For Pi (`ori pi`), Prime Agent (`ori prime-agent`), and DeepSeek Harness (`ori dsh`), Ori hooks the agent up to your own OpenRouter model catalog: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/ori/harness#live-model-catalog-and-routing-toggles
- [definition] Guardrails, on every agent — Set [guardrails](/docs/guides/features/guardrails), allowlists, and per-workspace permissions on your OpenRouter organization, and set [workspace budgets](/docs/guides/features/workspaces/workspace-budgets) there too. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/ori/harness#guardrails-on-every-agent
- [definition] One bill across agents — You pay for Ori traffic through OpenRouter's normal billing and activity reporting. You see it next to your other traffic in [Usage Accounting](/docs/cookbook/administration/usage-accounting) and [Activity Export](/docs/cookbook/administration/activity-export). — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/ori/harness#one-bill-across-agents
- [definition] Do I need an OpenRouter API key? — No. Ori signs you in with OAuth PKCE through your OpenRouter login. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/ori/harness#do-i-need-an-openrouter-api-key
- [definition] Do I need to change my agent workflow? — No. Keep the same agent, commands, and flags. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/ori/harness#do-i-need-to-change-my-agent-workflow
- [definition] Which agents are supported? — Claude Code (`ori claude`), Codex (`ori codex`), Grok Build (`ori grok`), Hermes (`ori hermes`), OpenCode (`ori opencode`), Pi (`ori pi`), Prime Agent (`ori prime-agent`), and DeepSeek Harness (`ori dsh`) work today, and more harnesses are coming. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/ori/harness#which-agents-are-supported

- [parameter] API key filter: API field=`allowed_api_key_hashes`; Type=`string[] \| null`; Semantics=Allowlist of OpenRouter API key hashes (the `hash` field from the [Keys API](/docs/api/api-reference/keys)). `null` means no restriction. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/auth/byok#managing-filters-via-the-management-api
- [parameter] Member filter: API field=`allowed_user_ids`; Type=`string[] \| null`; Semantics=Allowlist of user IDs (Clerk user IDs). `null` means no restriction. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/auth/byok#managing-filters-via-the-management-api
- [definition] Bring your own API Keys — OpenRouter supports both OpenRouter credits and the option to bring your own provider keys (BYOK). — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/auth/byok#bring-your-own-api-keys
- [definition] Key Priority and Fallback — Each BYOK key belongs to one of two sections: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/auth/byok#key-priority-and-fallback
- [definition] BYOK with Provider Ordering — When you combine BYOK keys with [provider ordering](/docs/guides/routing/provider-selection#ordering-specific-providers), OpenRouter **always prioritizes BYOK endpoints first**, regardless of where that provider appears in your specified order. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/auth/byok#byok-with-provider-ordering
- [definition] BYOK with Data Policies — BYOK endpoints are subject to your data policies. Bringing your own key changes which credential authenticates the upstream request. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/auth/byok#byok-with-data-policies
- [definition] BYOK and Guardrail Budgets — By default, BYOK inference spend does **not** count toward [guardrail](/docs/guides/features/guardrails) budgets. Only OpenRouter credit spend does. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/auth/byok#byok-and-guardrail-budgets
- [definition] BYOK and Workspace Budgets — [Workspace budgets](/docs/guides/features/workspaces/workspace-budgets) behave the same way and are controlled separately from guardrails. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/auth/byok#byok-and-workspace-budgets
- [definition] Multiple BYOK Keys for the Same Provider — You can configure multiple BYOK keys for the same provider. All matching keys are used for routing, and each key produces its own endpoint copy that is pinned to that specific key throughout the request lifecycle. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/auth/byok#multiple-byok-keys-for-the-same-provider
- [definition] Azure API Keys — Azure has two resource types, each using a different domain: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/auth/byok#azure-api-keys
- [definition] AWS Bedrock API Keys — To use Amazon Bedrock with OpenRouter, you can authenticate using either Bedrock API keys or traditional AWS credentials. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/auth/byok#aws-bedrock-api-keys
- [definition] Google Vertex API Keys — To use Google Vertex AI with OpenRouter, provide your Google Cloud service account key in JSON format. The key should include the standard Google Cloud service account fields, with an optional `region` for selecting the deployment region. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/auth/byok#google-vertex-api-keys
- [definition] Vertex Batch storage — [Batch API](/docs/batch-quickstart) Vertex BYOK stages input and reads Vertex output from a bucket in your own project. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/auth/byok#vertex-batch-storage
- [definition] Debugging BYOK Issues — If your BYOK requests fail, you can debug the issue by viewing provider responses on the Activity page. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/auth/byok#debugging-byok-issues

## MCP
<https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/mcp-server>

- [snippet] lines: claude mcp add --transport http openrouter https://mcp.openrouter.ai/mcp — `claude mcp add --transport http openrouter https://mcp.openrouter.ai/mcp` — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/mcp-server#connect-your-agent
- [snippet] lines: codex mcp add openrouter --url https://mcp.openrouter.ai/mcp — `codex mcp add openrouter --url https://mcp.openrouter.ai/mcp` — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/mcp-server#connect-your-agent
- [snippet] lines: { — `{` — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/mcp-server#connect-your-agent
- [snippet] lines: { — `{` — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/mcp-server#connect-your-agent
- [parameter] `send-message`: Send a message to any model and get its reply, to test a prompt or compare models — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/mcp-server#what-you-can-do
- [parameter] `generate-image`: Generate an image from a text prompt and get it back inline as an image content block — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/mcp-server#what-you-can-do
- [parameter] `list-models`: Search OpenRouter's live model catalog: free-text search, sort (including by Artificial Analysis intelligence, coding, and agentic indexes and Design Arena ELO), and filter by use case, prompt/completion price, minimum context, model age, benchmark index ranges, tool-calling success rate, model family, author, provider, input/output modality, supported parameters, and ZDR or region — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/mcp-server#what-you-can-do
- [parameter] `get-model`: Full details for one model by `author/slug` (supports `:variant` suffixes and aliases) — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/mcp-server#what-you-can-do
- [parameter] `list-model-endpoints`: Which providers serve a model, and their price, latency, throughput, and data policy — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/mcp-server#what-you-can-do
- [parameter] `list-providers`: List available providers for routing preferences — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/mcp-server#what-you-can-do
- [parameter] `list-daily-model-rankings`: Which models are most used and trending by token volume — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/mcp-server#what-you-can-do
- [parameter] `list-app-rankings`: Which apps drive the most OpenRouter traffic, filterable by category — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/mcp-server#what-you-can-do
- [parameter] `get-credits`: Your remaining account credit — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/mcp-server#what-you-can-do
- [parameter] `get-generation`: Cost, token counts, and serving provider for a specific generation id — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/mcp-server#what-you-can-do
- [parameter] `list-benchmarks`: Third-party quality scores from Artificial Analysis (intelligence, coding, agentic indexes) and Design Arena (head-to-head elo, win rate) — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/mcp-server#what-you-can-do
- [parameter] `list-task-classifications`: What OpenRouter traffic is used for: market share by task type (code generation, web search, summarization, …) with the top models for each and macro-category (Code, Data, Agent, General) aggregates — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/mcp-server#what-you-can-do
- [parameter] `search-docs`: Search the full OpenRouter docs to answer "how do I…" questions — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/mcp-server#what-you-can-do
- [parameter] `send-feedback`: Report a problem with one of your own generations (category + optional comment), sent to the OpenRouter team — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/mcp-server#what-you-can-do
- [parameter] `spawn-ori-eval`: Get the instructions for running a model eval with Ori (your own agent on your own prompts, on a pinned harness and model), then follow them — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/mcp-server#what-you-can-do
- [parameter] `install-ori-harness`: Get the argument-free recipe for installing the Ori harness and follow it — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/mcp-server#what-you-can-do
- [parameter] `ping`: Health check to verify the connection — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/mcp-server#what-you-can-do
- [definition] MCP — Connect your AI coding tools to OpenRouter over MCP — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/mcp-server#mcp
- [definition] What you can do — The MCP exposes these tools. Most are read-only lookups against live OpenRouter data. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/mcp-server#what-you-can-do
- [definition] Pick the right model for a task — You describe a task and the assistant recommends a model for it, with the recommendation backed by live data rather than the model's stale training knowledge. `send-message` is grounded so the assistant won't name a model from memory. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/mcp-server#pick-the-right-model-for-a-task
- [definition] How it works — 1. **Discovery & auth.** An unauthenticated request returns a `401` that points your client to OpenRouter's OAuth authorization server. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/mcp-server#how-it-works

## Multimodal Capabilities
<https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/multimodal/overview>

- [definition] Multimodal Capabilities — Send images, PDFs, audio, and video to OpenRouter models, generate speech from text, or transcribe audio to text — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/multimodal/overview#multimodal-capabilities
- [definition] Images — Send images to vision-capable models for analysis, description, OCR, and more. OpenRouter supports multiple image formats and both URL-based and base64-encoded images. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/multimodal/overview#images
- [definition] Image Generation — Generate images from text prompts using AI models with image output capabilities. OpenRouter supports various image generation models that can create high-quality images based on your descriptions. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/multimodal/overview#image-generation
- [definition] PDFs — Process PDF documents with any model on OpenRouter. Our intelligent PDF parsing system extracts text and handles both text-based and scanned documents. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/multimodal/overview#pdfs
- [definition] Audio — Send audio files to speech-capable models for transcription, analysis, and processing, or receive audio responses from models with audio output capabilities. OpenRouter supports common audio formats for both input and output. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/multimodal/overview#audio
- [definition] Video — Send video files to video-capable models for analysis, description, object detection, and action recognition. OpenRouter supports multiple video formats for comprehensive video understanding tasks. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/multimodal/overview#video
- [definition] Video Generation — Generate videos from text prompts using AI models with video output capabilities. OpenRouter supports an asynchronous video generation API with configurable resolution, aspect ratio, duration, and optional reference images. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/multimodal/overview#video-generation
- [definition] Text-to-Speech — Generate speech audio from text using a dedicated OpenAI-compatible endpoint. OpenRouter supports multiple TTS providers and voices with output in MP3 or PCM format. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/multimodal/overview#text-to-speech
- [definition] Speech-to-Text — Transcribe audio into text using a dedicated endpoint. OpenRouter supports multiple STT providers and models, returning structured JSON with transcribed text and usage statistics. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/multimodal/overview#speech-to-text
- [definition] Getting Started — Most multimodal inputs use the same `/api/v1/chat/completions` endpoint with the `messages` parameter. Different content types are specified in the message content array: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/multimodal/overview#getting-started
- [definition] Model Compatibility — Not all models support every modality. OpenRouter automatically filters available models based on your request content: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/multimodal/overview#model-compatibility
- [definition] Input Format Support — OpenRouter supports both **direct URLs** and **base64-encoded data** for multimodal inputs: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/multimodal/overview#input-format-support

- [parameter] `completed`: The video is ready to download — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/multimodal/video-generation#job-statuses
- [parameter] `failed`: The generation failed (check the `error` field) — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/multimodal/video-generation#job-statuses
- [definition] Video Generation — How to generate videos with OpenRouter models — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/multimodal/video-generation#video-generation
- [definition] Model Discovery — You can find video generation models in several ways: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/multimodal/video-generation#model-discovery
- [definition] Via the Video Models API — Use the dedicated video models endpoint to list all available video generation models along with their supported parameters: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/multimodal/video-generation#via-the-video-models-api
- [definition] Via the Models API — You can also use the `output_modalities` query parameter on the [Models API](/docs/api/api-reference/models/list-all-models-and-their-properties) to discover video generation models: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/multimodal/video-generation#via-the-models-api

- [definition] How It Works — Unlike text or image generation, video generation is **asynchronous** because generating video takes significantly longer. The workflow is: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/multimodal/video-generation#how-it-works
- [definition] Using Images — There are two ways to provide images, each triggering a different generation mode: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/multimodal/video-generation#using-images
- [definition] Provider-Specific Options — You can pass provider-specific options using the `provider` parameter. - [definition] Webhooks — Instead of polling for job status, you can receive a webhook notification when a video generation job completes. There are two ways to configure a callback URL: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/multimodal/video-generation#webhooks
- [definition] Webhook Payload — When a job reaches a terminal state, OpenRouter sends a POST request to the callback URL with an event envelope. Each delivery also carries an `X-OpenRouter-Idempotency-Key` header of the form `<job_id>-<status>` for safe retry deduplication. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/multimodal/video-generation#webhook-payload
- [definition] Signing Secret — You can configure a signing secret in your [workspace settings](/docs/guides/features/workspaces) to verify that webhook payloads are authentically from OpenRouter. - [definition] Verifying Signatures — To verify the signature on your webhook receiver: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/multimodal/video-generation#verifying-signatures
- [definition] Zero Data Retention — Video generation is **not eligible** for [Zero Data Retention (ZDR)](/docs/guides/features/zdr). Because video generation is asynchronous, the provider must retain the generated video output briefly so you can retrieve it after generation completes. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/multimodal/video-generation#zero-data-retention
