## Auto Exacto
<https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/auto-exacto>

- [snippet] lines: new Validator(parameters, '7') — `new Validator(parameters, '7')` — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/auto-exacto#validator
- [snippet] Request-level aggregation: requests_with_tool_call_errors / requests_where_finish_reason_is_tool_calls — `requests_with_tool_call_errors / requests_where_finish_reason_is_tool_calls` — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/auto-exacto#request-level-aggregation
- [definition] Auto Exacto — Automatic tool-calling provider optimization — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/auto-exacto#auto-exacto
- [definition] How it works — When your request includes tools, Auto Exacto reorders the available providers for your chosen model using a combination of real-world performance signals: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/auto-exacto#how-it-works
- [definition] How tool-calling success rate is measured — The tool-calling success rate signal is derived from the **Tool Call Error Rate** metric, which is also visible on the Performance tab of any model page. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/auto-exacto#how-tool-calling-success-rate-is-measured
- [definition] Validator — Tool call `arguments` are validated against the corresponding `tools[].function.parameters` schema using [`@cfworker/json-schema`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@cfworker/json-schema), pinned to **JSON Schema Draft 7**: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/auto-exacto#validator
- [definition] Regex engine — `@cfworker/json-schema` delegates `pattern` and `patternProperties` to the runtime's built-in regex implementation. In OpenRouter's environment that is the native JavaScript `RegExp` (V8 / ECMA-262). — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/auto-exacto#regex-engine
- [definition] Per-tool-call classification — Each tool call is bucketed into one of three error categories, or counted as valid: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/auto-exacto#per-tool-call-classification
- [definition] Request-level aggregation — A request is flagged as errored if **any** of its tool calls falls into one of the three buckets above. The Tool Call Error Rate displayed per endpoint per day is then computed at the **request** level. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/auto-exacto#request-level-aggregation
- [definition] What the benchmark harness runs — The benchmark signal comes from OpenRouter's in-house benchmark harness, which runs on a recurring schedule against every provider endpoint serving an enrolled model. Two benchmarks currently feed Auto Exacto routing: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/auto-exacto#what-the-benchmark-harness-runs
- [definition] How the benchmark threshold is set — Each model and benchmark type has a baseline: the median of per-endpoint scores during the first approximately 21 days of benchmarking for that model and benchmark type. The derank threshold is that baseline minus **2σ**. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/auto-exacto#how-the-benchmark-threshold-is-set
- [definition] Results — OpenRouter has measured improvements in [tau-bench](https://github.com/sierra-research/tau-bench) scores and tool-calling success rates on tool-calling requests routed through Auto Exacto. See the AutoExacto Benchmarks card on each enrolled model page for per-endpoint numbers. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/auto-exacto#results
- [definition] Interaction with Prompt Caching — Auto Exacto reorders providers on every tool-calling request, which can conflict with the sticky routing used by [prompt caching](/docs/guides/best-practices/prompt-caching). — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/auto-exacto#interaction-with-prompt-caching
- [definition] Opting out — Without Auto Exacto, OpenRouter's default routing is primarily [price-weighted](/docs/guides/routing/provider-selection#price-based-load-balancing-default-strategy). Requests are load balanced across providers with a strong preference for lower cost. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/auto-exacto#opting-out

## Exacto Variant
<https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/model-variants/exacto>

- [snippet] title="TypeScript SDK" lines: import { OpenRouter } from '@openrouter/sdk'; — `import { OpenRouter } from '@openrouter/sdk';` — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/model-variants/exacto#using-the-exacto-variant
- [snippet] title="TypeScript (OpenAI SDK)" lines: import OpenAI from "openai"; — `import OpenAI from "openai";` — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/model-variants/exacto#using-the-exacto-variant
- [snippet] title="cURL" lines: curl https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions \ — `curl https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions \` — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/model-variants/exacto#using-the-exacto-variant
- [definition] Exacto Variant — Route requests with quality-first provider sorting — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/model-variants/exacto#exacto-variant
- [definition] Using the Exacto variant — Add `:exacto` to the end of any supported model slug. This is a shortcut for setting the provider sort to Exacto on that model. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/model-variants/exacto#using-the-exacto-variant
- [definition] What is the Exacto variant? — Exacto is a routing shortcut for quality-first provider ordering. Unlike standard routing, which primarily favors lower-cost providers, Exacto prefers providers with stronger signals for tool-calling reliability and deprioritizes weaker performers. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/model-variants/exacto#what-is-the-exacto-variant
- [definition] Why we built it — Providers serving the same model can vary meaningfully in tool-use behavior. Exacto gives you an explicit, request-level way to prefer higher-quality providers when you care more about tool-calling reliability than the default price-weighted route. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/model-variants/exacto#why-we-built-it
- [definition] Recommended use cases — Exacto is useful for quality-sensitive, agentic workflows where tool-calling accuracy and reliability matter more than raw cost efficiency. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/model-variants/exacto#recommended-use-cases
- [definition] How Exacto works — Exacto uses the same provider-ranking signals as [Auto Exacto](/docs/guides/routing/auto-exacto), but applies them explicitly because you chose the `:exacto` suffix. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/model-variants/exacto#how-exacto-works
- [definition] Supported models — Exacto is a virtual variant and is not backed by a separate endpoint pool. It can be used anywhere provider sorting is meaningful, especially on models with multiple compatible providers. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/model-variants/exacto#supported-models

In addition to the price sort, `:floor` makes [flex service tier](/docs/guides/features/service-tiers) endpoints eligible for the request, so it is a superset of setting `provider.sort` to `"price"` (which only sorts). — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/provider-selection#floor-price-shortcut
- [definition] Advanced Sorting with Partition — When using [model fallbacks](/docs/guides/routing/routers/auto-router), the `sort` field can be specified as an object with additional options to control how endpoints are sorted across multiple models. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/provider-selection#advanced-sorting-with-partition
- [definition] Use Case 1: Route to the Highest Throughput or Lowest Latency Model — When you have multiple acceptable models and want to use whichever has the best performance right now, use `partition: "none"` with throughput or latency sorting. This is useful when you care more about speed than using a specific model. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/provider-selection#use-case-1-route-to-the-highest-throughput-or-lowest-latency-model
- [definition] Performance Thresholds — You can set minimum throughput or maximum latency thresholds to filter endpoints. Endpoints that don't meet these thresholds are deprioritized (moved to the end of the list) rather than excluded entirely. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/provider-selection#performance-thresholds
- [definition] How Percentiles Work — OpenRouter tracks latency and throughput metrics for each model and provider using percentile statistics calculated over a rolling 5-minute window. The available percentiles are: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/provider-selection#how-percentiles-work
- [definition] When to Use Percentile Preferences — Percentile-based routing is useful when you need predictable performance characteristics: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/provider-selection#when-to-use-percentile-preferences
- [definition] Use Case 2: Find the Cheapest Model Meeting Performance Requirements — Combine `partition: "none"` with performance thresholds to find the cheapest option across multiple models that meets your performance requirements. This is useful when you have a performance floor but want to minimize costs. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/provider-selection#use-case-2-find-the-cheapest-model-meeting-performance-requirements
- [definition] Example: Using Multiple Percentile Cutoffs — You can specify multiple percentile cutoffs to set both typical and worst-case performance requirements. All specified cutoffs must be met for a model and provider to be in the preferred group. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/provider-selection#example-using-multiple-percentile-cutoffs
- [definition] Use Case 3: Maximize BYOK Usage Across Models — If you use [Bring Your Own Key (BYOK)](/docs/guides/overview/auth/byok) and want to maximize usage of your own API keys, `partition: "none"` can help. When your primary model doesn't have a BYOK provider available, OpenRouter can route to a fallback model that does support BYOK. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/provider-selection#use-case-3-maximize-byok-usage-across-models
- [definition] Ordering Specific Providers — You can set the providers that OpenRouter will prioritize for your request using the `order` field. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/provider-selection#ordering-specific-providers
- [definition] Example: Specifying providers with fallbacks — This example skips over OpenAI (which doesn't host Mixtral), tries Together, and then falls back to the normal list of providers on OpenRouter: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/provider-selection#example-specifying-providers-with-fallbacks
- [definition] Example: Specifying providers with fallbacks disabled — Here's an example with `allow_fallbacks` set to `false` that skips over OpenAI (which doesn't host Mixtral), tries Together, and then fails if Together fails: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/provider-selection#example-specifying-providers-with-fallbacks-disabled
- [definition] Targeting Specific Provider Endpoints — Each provider on OpenRouter may host multiple endpoints for the same model, such as a default endpoint and a specialized "turbo" endpoint, or region-specific endpoints like `google-vertex/us-east5`. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/provider-selection#targeting-specific-provider-endpoints
- [definition] Base Slug Matching — When you use a base provider slug (e.g. `"google-vertex"`) in any provider routing field (`order`, `only`, or `ignore`), it matches **all** endpoints for that provider, including any variants or regions. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/provider-selection#base-slug-matching
- [definition] Example: Targeting a specific endpoint variant — For example, DeepInfra offers DeepSeek R1 through multiple endpoints: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/provider-selection#example-targeting-a-specific-endpoint-variant
- [definition] Requiring Providers to Support All Parameters — You can restrict requests only to providers that support all parameters in your request using the `require_parameters` field. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/provider-selection#requiring-providers-to-support-all-parameters
- [definition] Default parameter preferences — Even when `require_parameters` is `false`, a small set of parameters is used as a soft preference when choosing between providers of the same model: `tools`, `response_format` (including structured outputs), and `verbosity`. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/provider-selection#default-parameter-preferences
- [definition] Example: Excluding providers that don't support JSON formatting — For example, to only use providers that support JSON formatting: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/provider-selection#example-excluding-providers-that-dont-support-json-formatting
- [definition] Requiring Providers to Comply with Data Policies — You can restrict requests only to providers that comply with your data policies using the `data_collection` field. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/provider-selection#requiring-providers-to-comply-with-data-policies
- [definition] Example: Excluding providers that don't comply with data policies — To exclude providers that don't comply with your data policies, set `data_collection` to `deny`: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/provider-selection#example-excluding-providers-that-dont-comply-with-data-policies
- [definition] Zero Data Retention Enforcement — You can enforce Zero Data Retention (ZDR) on a per-request basis using the `zdr` parameter, ensuring your request only routes to endpoints that do not retain prompts. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/provider-selection#zero-data-retention-enforcement
- [definition] Example: Enforcing ZDR for a specific request — To ensure a request only uses ZDR endpoints, set `zdr` to `true`: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/provider-selection#example-enforcing-zdr-for-a-specific-request

- [definition] Disabling Fallbacks — To guarantee that your request is only served by the top (lowest-cost) provider, you can disable fallbacks. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/provider-selection#disabling-fallbacks
- [definition] Allowing Only Specific Providers — You can allow only specific providers for a request by setting the `only` field in the `provider` object. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/provider-selection#allowing-only-specific-providers

- [definition] Quantization — Quantization reduces model size and computational requirements while aiming to preserve performance. Most LLMs today use FP16 or BF16 for training and inference, cutting memory requirements in half compared to FP32. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/provider-selection#quantization
- [definition] Quantization Levels — By default, requests are load-balanced across all available providers, ordered by price. - [definition] Provider-Specific Headers — Some providers support beta features that can be enabled through special headers. - [parameter] `analysis_models`: Default=Quality preset (`~anthropic/claude-opus-latest`, `~openai/gpt-latest`, `~google/gemini-pro-latest`); Description=Models that form the panel. Each runs in parallel with `openrouter:web_search` and `openrouter:web_fetch` enabled. 1–8 models allowed. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/routers/fusion-router#tool-config-when-using-your-own-outer-model
- [parameter] `model`: Default=Your outer model; Description=The analyst model that produces the structured analysis JSON. Defaults to the same model handling your request. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/routers/fusion-router#tool-config-when-using-your-own-outer-model
- [parameter] `max_tool_calls`: Default=`4`; Description=Max tool-calling steps each panel model and the analyst may take in their `openrouter:web_search` / `openrouter:web_fetch` loop before they must return text. Range 1–16. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/routers/fusion-router#tool-config-when-using-your-own-outer-model
- [parameter] `max_completion_tokens`: Default=`16000`; Description=Max output tokens (including reasoning) per inner panel/analyst call. Keeps reasoning-heavy models from exhausting their budget before producing visible text. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/routers/fusion-router#tool-config-when-using-your-own-outer-model
- [parameter] `reasoning`: Default=Provider default; Description=Reasoning config forwarded to the panel and analyst calls: an object with optional `effort` and `max_tokens`. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/routers/fusion-router#tool-config-when-using-your-own-outer-model
- [parameter] `temperature`: Default=Provider default; Description=Temperature (`0`–`2`) forwarded to the panel calls. The analyst always runs at temperature 0. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/routers/fusion-router#tool-config-when-using-your-own-outer-model
- [definition] Fusion Router — Multi-model deliberation as a model slug — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/routers/fusion-router#fusion-router
- [definition] Overview — Use Fusion when a single model isn't enough: research questions, expert critique, "compare and contrast" prompts, or anything where the cost of being wrong outweighs the cost of a few extra completions. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/routers/fusion-router#overview
- [definition] Fast preset model: `openrouter/fusion-flash` — `openrouter/fusion-flash` is a separately-listed model that runs the fusion pipeline with the `general-fast` preset pre-selected, a latency-homogeneous panel tuned for fast agentic turns. When you don't pin your own fusion config, these two requests behave the same: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/routers/fusion-router#fast-preset-model-openrouterfusion-flash
- [definition] Configuration — Override the default panel and analyst for a Fusion run via the `plugins` array or the `tools` array. Both are optional; omit them entirely and fusion uses the Quality preset defaults. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/routers/fusion-router#configuration
- [definition] Plugin config (recommended with the model slug) — Pass a `fusion` plugin entry alongside `model: "openrouter/fusion"`. This is the same pattern the [Pareto Router](/docs/guides/routing/routers/pareto-router) uses for `min_coding_score`. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/routers/fusion-router#plugin-config-recommended-with-the-model-slug
- [definition] Tool config (when using your own outer model) — When you bring your own model and add `openrouter:fusion` as a server tool, configure it via the `tools` array instead: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/routers/fusion-router#tool-config-when-using-your-own-outer-model
- [definition] Forcing fusion on every request — By default, the model decides when to call `openrouter:fusion`. To guarantee it runs on every request, set `tool_choice: "required"`: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/routers/fusion-router#forcing-fusion-on-every-request
- [definition] Response — The response `model` field reports the **concrete model** that handled the request, not the `openrouter/fusion` alias: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/routers/fusion-router#response
- [definition] Cost — Fusion runs N panel calls + 1 analyst call in addition to your normal request. With the default 3-model panel, expect roughly 4–5× the cost of a single completion on the same prompt. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/routers/fusion-router#cost
- [definition] Recursion protection — Inner fusion calls carry an `x-openrouter-fusion-depth` header. Panel and analyst models cannot recursively invoke `openrouter:fusion`. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/routers/fusion-router#recursion-protection

<https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/routers/latest-resolution>

- [snippet] title="TypeScript SDK" lines: import { OpenRouter } from '@openrouter/sdk'; — `import { OpenRouter } from '@openrouter/sdk';` — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/routers/latest-resolution#usage

- [snippet] title="cURL" lines: curl https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions \ — `curl https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions \` — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/routers/latest-resolution#usage

- [snippet] lines: { — `{` — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/routers/latest-resolution#pinning-to-a-specific-version
- [definition] Latest Model Resolution — Always target the newest version of a model family with a single slug — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/routers/latest-resolution#latest-model-resolution
- [definition] Overview — When a model author ships a new version (for example Anthropic releasing `claude-opus-4.8`), OpenRouter automatically starts routing `~anthropic/claude-opus-latest` to it. Older code calling the alias keeps working. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/routers/latest-resolution#overview
- [definition] Usage — Send a chat completion request with a `~author/family-latest` slug as the model: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/routers/latest-resolution#usage
- [definition] Response — The response's `model` field reflects the concrete model that actually served the request, not the alias you sent. This makes it trivial to log or alert on version rollovers: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/routers/latest-resolution#response
- [definition] How it works — Each `~author/family-latest` slug is mapped to a model family on OpenRouter. When a request comes in: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/routers/latest-resolution#how-it-works
- [definition] Pricing and capabilities — `~author/family-latest` rows on the [models page](https://openrouter.ai/models) and in `/api/v1/models` responses report the pricing, context length, modalities, and supported parameters of the target they currently resolve to, not a frozen snapshot. This way: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/routers/latest-resolution#pricing-and-capabilities
- [definition] Compatibility contract — `~latest` slugs trade exactness for continuity. Your existing request shape keeps working when the alias retargets, even if the new model doesn't support every parameter you send. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/routers/latest-resolution#compatibility-contract
- [definition] Pinning to a specific version — When you need reproducibility, bypass latest resolution by calling the concrete model slug directly: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/routers/latest-resolution#pinning-to-a-specific-version

## Pareto Router
<https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/routers/pareto-router>

- [snippet] title="TypeScript SDK" expandable lines: import { OpenRouter } from '@openrouter/sdk'; — `import { OpenRouter } from '@openrouter/sdk';` — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/routers/pareto-router#usage
- [snippet] title="cURL" lines: curl https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions \ — `curl https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions \` — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/routers/pareto-router#usage
- [snippet] lines: { — `{` — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/routers/pareto-router#response
- [snippet] title="TypeScript SDK" expandable lines: const completion = await openRouter.chat.send({ — `const completion = await openRouter.chat.send({` — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/routers/pareto-router#example-with-session-id
- [snippet] title="cURL" lines: curl https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions \ — `curl https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions \` — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/routers/pareto-router#example-with-session-id
- [parameter] `>= 0.66`: Tier=high; AA coding percentile band=top of AA's coding field — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/routers/pareto-router#the-min-coding-score-parameter
- [parameter] `>= 0.33`, `< 0.66`: Tier=medium; AA coding percentile band=strong modern flagships below the top — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/routers/pareto-router#the-min-coding-score-parameter
- [parameter] `< 0.33`: Tier=low; AA coding percentile band=capable coders that still beat AA's median — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/routers/pareto-router#the-min-coding-score-parameter
- [parameter] omitted: Tier=high (default); AA coding percentile band=top of AA's coding field — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/routers/pareto-router#the-min-coding-score-parameter
- [definition] Pareto Router — Pick a coding model by minimum coding score without choosing a specific model — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/routers/pareto-router#pareto-router
- [definition] Overview — The Pareto Router is tuned for coding use cases. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/routers/pareto-router#overview
- [definition] Usage — Set your model to `openrouter/pareto-code` and optionally pass the `pareto-router` plugin to control the minimum coding score: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/routers/pareto-router#usage
- [definition] Default Settings — Instead of passing the `pareto-router` plugin on every API request, you can configure a default `min_coding_score` in the dashboard: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/routers/pareto-router#default-settings
- [definition] The `min_coding_score` parameter — `min_coding_score` is an optional number between `0` and `1`, where `1` is best. The router maps it to one of three quality tiers, and each tier corresponds to a percentile band on [Artificial Analysis](https://artificialanalysis.ai/) coding scores. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/routers/pareto-router#the-min-coding-score-parameter
- [definition] Response — The response includes the `model` field showing which coding model was actually used: — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/routers/pareto-router#response
- [definition] How It Works — 1. **Tier resolution**: Your `min_coding_score` value is mapped to one of three tiers (`high`, `medium`, `low`) using the thresholds in the table above. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/routers/pareto-router#how-it-works
- [definition] Session Stickiness — The Pareto Router reuses the selected **model** and **provider** on a best-effort basis so that subsequent requests in the same conversation route to the same place. This keeps behavior consistent within a conversation and maximizes [prompt cache](/docs/guides/best-practices/prompt-caching) hits. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/routers/pareto-router#session-stickiness
- [definition] Why It Matters for the Pareto Router — The Pareto Router selects a model based on coding score and cost — different requests could resolve to different models as the shortlist evolves. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/routers/pareto-router#why-it-matters-for-the-pareto-router
- [definition] Pricing — The Pareto Router itself adds no fee. You pay only for the underlying model that handles the request. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/routers/pareto-router#pricing

- [definition] Using the OpenRouter API — The most direct way to use OpenRouter. Send standard HTTP requests to the `/api/v1/chat/completions` endpoint. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/quickstart#using-the-openrouter-api
- [definition] Using the Client SDKs — The [Client SDKs](/docs/client-sdks/overview) wrap the OpenRouter API with full type safety, auto-generated types from the OpenAPI spec, and zero boilerplate. It's intentionally lean, a thin layer over the REST API. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/quickstart#using-the-client-sdks
- [definition] Using the Agent SDK — The [Agent SDK](/docs/agent-sdk/overview) (`@openrouter/agent`) provides higher-level primitives for building AI agents. It handles multi-turn conversation loops, tool execution, and state management automatically via the `callModel` function. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/quickstart#using-the-agent-sdk
- [definition] Using the OpenAI SDK — You can also use the OpenAI SDK pointed at OpenRouter as a drop-in replacement. This is useful if you have existing code built on the OpenAI SDK and want to access OpenRouter's model catalog without changing your code structure. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/quickstart#using-the-openai-sdk
- [definition] Using third-party SDKs — For information about using third-party SDKs and frameworks with OpenRouter, please [see our frameworks documentation.](/docs/guides/community/frameworks-and-integrations-overview) — https://openrouter.ai/docs/quickstart#using-third-party-sdks
- [definition] Building with an AI assistant — If you write code with an AI coding tool (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, and others), connect the [OpenRouter MCP server](/docs/guides/overview/mcp-server). It's a remote server hosted by OpenRouter, so there's nothing to install. — https://openrouter.ai/docs/quickstart#building-with-an-ai-assistant
